### Method for Determining Instantaneous Position

Now, he describes the procedure for finding the **instantaneous position of a planet** <term>tātkālika-karaṇa</term>:

"The **daily motion** <term>bhukti</term> multiplied by the **desired time-units** <term>iṣṭa-nāḍī</term> and divided by sixty gives the **arc-minutes** <term>kalā</term> and further units. These are to be subtracted if the time has passed, or added if the time is yet to come; thus, the instantaneous position is found."

By multiplying the **mean motion** <term>madhyama-gati</term> of the planet by the **desired time-units** <term>iṣṭa-ghaṭī</term> <note>A ghati is a unit of 24 minutes; there are 60 ghatis in a day</note> and dividing by **sixty** <term>ṣaṣṭyā</term>, the result is in arc-minutes and seconds. If the desired time is before midnight, this result is subtracted from the planet's known position; if the desired time is after midnight, the result is added to the planet's position. 

In this way, the **instantaneous planet** <term>tātkālika-graha</term>—the planet at one's specific desired time—is found. If the zodiac cycle has been adjusted, the reverse should be understood. A **true planet** <term>spaṣṭa-graha</term> derived from the **adjusted mean planet** <term>cālita-madhya-graha</term> is much more precise. If one attempts to calculate by moving a true planet using its **true motion** <term>spaṣṭa-gati</term>, the result will be "coarse" or less accurate. According to the three major traditions <note>likely the Surya, Arya, and Brahma Siddhantas</note>, adjusting the position starting from the mean motion is the proper method. Although some claim that because the difference is small, one can move the true planet by its true motion, this is not the true **scientific intent** <term>śāstrārtha</term>.

**Example:** 
Now, suppose the desired time for a planet is 10 [ghatis]. Let the **mean motion of the Sun** <term>sūryasya madhyama-gati</term> be 59 [minutes] 8 [seconds]. 
Multiplying 59 by 10, we get 590. 
Dividing by **sixty** <term>ṣaṣṭyā</term>, the result in **arc-minutes** <term>kalā</term> is 9 [minutes] 50 [seconds]. 
When this is added to the **Sun** <term>ravi</term>, the **instantaneous Sun** <term>tātkālika-ravi</term> is produced as 1 [sign] 5 [degrees] 7 [minutes] 13 [seconds]...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of planetary motion according to the Surya Siddhanta. Having established that the Pravaha wind provides the general westward motion, the text now explains the specific "pulling" forces—the attraction and repulsion—exerted by the deities of the High Points (apogees) and the Nodes, which account for the variation between a planet's mean position and its observed position.</meta>

The attraction and repulsion <note>original: "samāgopakarṣa," referring to the forces that pull a planet away from its mean path</note> are now described, as they clarify the impurities or discrepancies <note>original: "aśuddhi-bodhina," meaning the errors in calculating the true position versus the mean position</note> found in those [planetary paths]. Here, the following is explained in detail:

When a planet is in the **first half of its revolution** <term>bhagaṇārdha</term>, the entity known as the **High Point** <term>ucca-saṃjñā</term> pulls the planet eastward <note>original: "prāṅmukhaṃ karṣati"</note>. The deity specifically designated as the **High Point** stands in the first six signs—half the circle—and being situated ahead by a distance of up to six signs, he faces that direction and pulls the planetary orb <term>vimba</term>. This means he moves it forward from its mean position.

Conversely, when the planet is in the **latter half-revolution** <note>original: "aparārdhasya," the second six signs of the circle</note>, the deity known as the **High Point** stands behind the planet by a distance of up to six signs. In this case, he pulls the planetary orb toward the west <note>original: "paścimābhimukhaṃ," facing westward</note>. This means he moves it backward from its mean position.

Now, the author explains the result of this action:

> Drawn from the sky <note>original: "khāccāpakṛṣṭā," pulled from its empty or mean position</note> by those revolutions <note>here referring to the "reins" or cords of force</note>, whatever distance a planet is moved every day, that amount is applied to them as an **addition** or a **subtraction**.

In the first case <note>when pulled eastward</note>, it will be ahead. Due to the position within the revolution, according to the former arrangement, the planetary disks are pulled by the deity; the distance they travel in the circle each day is the amount of the correction. When calculating the longitude in signs and degrees, if it is ahead, the result is an **addition** <term>dhana</term> <note>original: "dhana," meaning a positive correction to the mean longitude</note>.

In the second case, when it is said to be "westward-facing" <note>original: "paścānmukhe"</note>, meaning it has been pulled back, then in the calculation of the longitude in signs and degrees, the result is a **subtraction** <term>ṛṇa</term> <note>original: "ṛṇa," meaning a negative correction to the mean longitude</note>.

Furthermore, having supported the existence of these eastward and westward movements, he explains that a two-fold movement in the **north and south** directions is also possible, caused by the **Node** <term>pāta</term>:

> In the same way, the **Node** [pulls the planet] toward the south and north...

The commentary <note>original: "mūṃ si haḥ," likely an abbreviation for the Mula-Siddhanta or a specific commentator's name</note> states: By its own velocity, the Nodes throw the planets off their paths. **Siddhānta Śiromaṇi, Section 18**; as stated in the eighth [verse], the first **half-sine segment** <term>jyārdha-khaṇḍa</term> is measured by the *Elements* <note>Tattva = 25</note> and the *Twin Gods* <note>Ashvins = 2</note>, which is **225**. This is derived from the circumference of the circle of signs <note>the zodiac</note> measured in minutes <term>kalā</term>. By taking the ninety-sixth part of the seven-fold [circumference], one obtains the measure of a single arc segment in minutes, which is **225**.

Because the arc and the sine are nearly equal when the angle is small, the first sine segment is established as **225**. Then, according to the stated method, when the cumulative sums <term>piṇḍāḥ</term> <note>the total sine values calculated so far</note> are divided by 225, the quotient obtained is **1**. 

By this [quotient]—having subtracted it from the previous segment—the subsequent differences between segments are produced. Thus, by subtracting the quotient **1** from the first segment of **225**, the second segment difference becomes **222**. <note>The standard calculation usually yields 224; 222 may represent a specific variant or scribal tradition.</note>

By adding this, the second [cumulative] sine segment becomes **447**. Again, dividing this sum by the initial value [225], the quotient obtained is **3**. Subtracting this from the previous difference of **222**, the third segment difference becomes **219**. Adding this [to the previous total], the third [cumulative] segment becomes **850** <note>This value 850 is unusual for R=3438; it likely refers to a different radius or a transcription error for 671.</note>, and the fifth segment becomes **1105**.

In this manner, the generation of the segments proceeds. These twenty-four segments of the sine-arc are calculated in sequence; this is the clear meaning. (15)

Now he explains the method for finding the declination <term>Kranti</term> by means of the maximum declination sine <term>Paramapakramajya</term>. 

Where the sine of maximum declination is followed, the declination is produced there. In that context, the arc derived from the sine, divided by the radius, is called the declination <term>Kranti</term>.

The maximum declination <term>Paramapakramajya</term> is twenty-four degrees <note>24° was the standard value for the obliquity of the ecliptic in ancient and medieval Indian astronomy, representing the tilt of the Earth's axis</note>.

The resulting value is then converted into an arc <term>Chapa-dhanus</term>, which is called the declination <term>Kranti</term>. This is according to the principles of the "Science of the Spheres" <note>Gola-tattva</note>.

### Finding Sine and Cosine via the Anomaly

Now, for the sake of obtaining the result, he explains the method for finding the sine <term>Bhujajya</term> or <term>Doh-jya</term> and the cosine <term>Kotijya</term> by first calculating the "anomaly" <term>Kendra</term> and its quadrants. 

This involves the correction of the planet <note>Graha-samshodhana</note>. By applying the "fast" correction <term>Shighra</term> and others, and adding or subtracting these to the mean position, one finds the corrected position. From this, the sine and cosine are derived. 

By taking the corrected planet and the "fast" anomaly <term>Shighra-kendra</term>, and subtracting them as required, the remainder in both cases is the "anomaly" <term>Kendra</term>. 

From the quadrants <term>Pada</term> of this anomaly—three by three quadrants—the sine <term>Bhujajya</term> and the cosine <term>Kotijya</term> are to be known based on whether the quadrant is odd or even. This is the meaning.

Now, by this observation, within such an odd quadrant <term>Vishama-pada</term>, thereafter in the middle of the three signs up to the limit of the twelve signs—the complete circle of the twelve signs—Sine and Cosine are possible. How are they possible? To answer this, he says:

To calculate the Sine of a desired arc, one must first convert the arc into minutes <term>Lipta</term>. These should be divided by 225 <note>The "Elements" or Tattvas refer to the 25 principles of Samkhya philosophy, but in this mathematical context, the word is used as a mnemonic for the number 225</note>. The quotient represents the number of full Sine segments <term>Jya-pinda</term> that have been completed. The remainder, which represents the portion of the next segment yet to be covered, should be multiplied by the difference between the current segment and the next one. After dividing this by 225, the resulting value is added to the total of the completed segments. This gives the precise Sine for the elapsed arc. This calculation process for the Sine <term>Bhujajya</term> is also to be understood as the method for calculating Versed Sines <term>Utkramajya</term>.

## Now, the method for determining the Arc

Since the Sine was previously determined through the "Elements" <note>original: "Tattva," a numerical code for 225, representing the 3°45' intervals in standard Indian Sine tables</note>, the process is now described to find the arc from a given Sine value.

To find the arc of a desired Sine <term>Jya</term>, determine the greatest known Sine segment <note>from the table</note> that can be subtracted from it. Subtract that value, and take the remainder. Multiply this remainder by 125 <unclear>5</unclear> <note>The text appears to discuss the interpolation between Sine segments</note> or the "Elements" (225). Divide the result by the difference between the current Sine segment and the next segment. The resulting value, when added to the index of the subtracted segments, constitutes the Arc <term>Dhanu</term> in minutes. 225.

### Method for Calculating the Equation of Center

Thus, here he explains the method for achieving the correction known as the <term>Manda-phala</term> <note>the "slow-result" or equation of center, used to account for the eccentricity of an orbit</note> based on those circumferences:

The corresponding sine <term>Bhujajya</term> and cosine <term>Kotijya</term> are to be divided by the number of units in a circle. The arc of the resulting sine, when calculated for the <term>Manda</term> <note>slow/eccentric</note> process, gives the correction in minutes <term>Lipta-phala</term>.

One must calculate the sine <term>Bhujajya</term> and cosine <term>Kotijya</term> of the anomaly <term>Manda-kendra</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet from its apogee</note>. These should be multiplied by the corrected circumference <term>Sphuta-paridhi</term> and then divided by 360 <note>the degrees in a circle, referred to here as "Bhagana"</note>. This yields the results for the "arm" and the "upright" <note>the horizontal and vertical components of the calculation</note>.

In this process, the arc of the sine result <term>Bhujajya-phala-dhanus</term> must be determined. That value becomes the <term>Manda-phala</term> in minutes and further subdivisions.

### Determination of the Sine Based on Quadrants

The "arm" <term>Bhuja</term> used for the sine calculation is determined as follows: 
- If the position is less than three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, that value itself is the <term>Bhuja</term>. 
- If it is above three signs, it should be subtracted from six signs <note>180 degrees</note> to find the <term>Bhuja</term>. 
- If it is between six and nine signs <note>180 to 270 degrees</note>, one should subtract six signs from the value. 
- If it is between nine and twelve signs <note>270 to 360 degrees</note>, the value should be subtracted from twelve signs to find the <term>Bhuja</term>.

The remainder when subtracting this <term>Bhuja</term> from three signs <note>90 degrees</note> results in the cosine <term>Kotijya</term>. This follows the previously mentioned rules.

**2 Signs, 11 Degrees, 05 Minutes, 45 Seconds** (and 3 fractions of a second).

### Calculation of the Sine (Bhujajya)

The term "passed sine" <note>original: *gata-bhujajya*</note> is used here because the position falls within an odd quadrant. One must calculate the sine of the traversed arc. In this example, the arc traversed in the first odd quadrant is **112; 5, 52** <note>112 degrees, 5 minutes, and 52 seconds; or more likely expressed here in minutes and seconds of arc</note>.

This value of **112; 5, 52** is the "arm" <note>original: *bhuja*</note>. To find the sine:
1.  The value in minutes is **112; 5, 52**.
2.  Divide this by 225 <note>original: *tattva-yamaiḥ*, a numerical code where "elements" (*tattva*) are 25 and "twins" (*yama*) are 2, representing 225</note>.
3.  The quotient shows that **11** full sine segments have been passed.
4.  The value of the 11th passed sine segment is **2277**. 
5.  The value of the current (12th) segment to be calculated is **1531**.
6.  The difference between these two segments is **1695**.
7.  Multiply this difference by the remainder, which is **55; 52**. The result is **8512; 58**.
8.  Divide this by 225 <note>original: *tattva-locanaiḥ*, another code for 225</note>. The result is **392; 52**.
9.  Add this result to the value of the passed segments (**2277**).

The total **Sine** <note>original: *jya*</note> is thus **2309; 52**. 

### Calculation of the Versine (Utkramajya)

For the purpose of providing a complete example, the calculation of the **versine** <note>original: *utkramajya*; the "versed sine" or $R(1 - \cos \theta)$</note> is also performed. 

Using the same "arm" of **112; 5, 52**:
1.  Divide the minutes (**112; 5, 52**) by 225. 
2.  The number of passed versine segments is **11**, with a value of **853**. 
3.  The next segment (the 12th) has a value of **1003**. 
4.  The difference between them is **255**. 
5.  Multiply this difference by the remainder (**55; 52**). The result is **8513; 48**.
6.  Divide by 225. The result is **32; 16**.
7.  Add this to the passed versine segment value of **853**. 

The final **Versine** is **895; 22, 16**.

This is divided by the total number of minutes in a circle. The result of the sine calculation is 48; 15. When added to the sine sum, it becomes 88; 15. One unit is lost in the **sine segment** <note>original: *jyā-khaṇḍa*; the discrete intervals used in Sanskrit sine tables</note>, thus the remainder is 88; 15. 

There also, dividing by 225 <note>a standard interval of 3 degrees 45 minutes used in Indian trigonometry</note>, we get 1882125. Regarding the base segments, by the difference of the subsequent segments and dividing by 225, the result is 88; 15. This is multiplied by the "elements" <note>original: *tattva*, representing the number 25</note> and the "fire" <note>original: *asvi*, usually representing 2 or 3 in numerical code</note>. The final result obtained for the **Equation of Center** <term>original: *mandaphala*; the angular correction required due to the planet's elliptical orbit</term> is 88; 15. This is the **Equation of Center** in seconds and minutes.

### Now, the instruction for the knowledge of applying this result is stated:

In the calculation for all planets, when the **Anomaly** <term>original: *kendra*; the angular distance from the apogee</term> begins with **Aries** <note>the first six signs of the zodiac, from 0° to 180°</note>, the result is **additive** <term>original: *dhana*; literally "wealth" or plus</term> to the planets' positions in minutes and so on.

When the anomaly begins with **Libra** <note>the latter six signs of the zodiac, from 180° to 360°</note>, the result is **subtractive** <term>original: *ṛṇa*; literally "debt" or minus</term> for all planets. This is the explanation of the Aries-onward division.

<summary>This page concludes a complex trigonometric calculation to find the "Equation of Center" (Mandaphala) and provides the fundamental rule for applying this correction: add the result if the planet is in the first half of its orbit (Aries to Libra) and subtract it if in the second half.</summary>

### 88 15 || 50 || Now, he speaks of the correction for the equation of time <term>original: *bhujāntara*; a correction applied to the longitude of a planet to account for the difference between mean and true solar time</term> ||

The results of the Sun's equation of center <note>original: *arkabhāskara-lābha*</note> are multiplied by the daily motion of the planets <term>original: *graha-bhukti*; the distance a planet travels in one day</term> and divided by the minutes of the zodiac circle <note>original: *bhavacakra-kalā*; the 21,600 minutes that make up a full 360-degree circle</note>. These minutes of correction should be applied to the planets just as they are to the Sun. 

Regarding this, a certain modern scholar has said that all corrections of the base result <note>original: *bhuja-phala*</note> should be performed as a single combined operation. That is not correct here. The daily motion of the planet should be multiplied by the Sun's equation of center <note>original: *arka-bhāskara-phala*</note>. This results in the mean daily motion for the given day-count <note>original: *ahargaṇa-madhyama-bhukti*</note>. Dividing this by the minutes of the zodiac circle, the resulting minutes of the equation of time correction <note>original: *bhujāntara-kalā*</note> are applied to the planets in the same manner as the Sun. This means: if the Sun’s equation of center is additive (positive), then the correction to the planet's result must also be made additive.

**Example:**
For the Sun's equation of center, which is 88; 15, let it be multiplied by the Sun's mean daily motion of 59; 08. The product is 5221, 13, 31. Dividing this by the 21,600 minutes of the zodiac circle, the quotient obtained is 0; 14 minutes.

Now, for the Moon's mean daily motion of 790; 35 <note>OCR reads 7 50 3 5; 790 minutes is roughly 13° 10'</note>, it is multiplied by the Sun's equation of center, 88; 15. The product is 658251 <note>original: 6582 51</note>. Dividing by the minutes of the zodiac circle, the quotient obtained is 3; 23.

In this way, having calculated the equation of time corrections for all the planets, they are written down:

| Sun | Moon | Apex | Mars | Merc. | Jup. | Ven. | Sat. | Node |

| 00 | 17 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 | 00 |
| 15 | 13 | 01 | 71 | 01 | 01 | 13 | 00 | 03 |
| 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 |

Regarding the results produced by the movement of planets at **Lanka-midnight** <term>original: *lankārdharātra*; the traditional prime meridian of Indian astronomy, conceptually located on the equator</term>, no correction should be performed there. This is because, within the timeframe of a solar fortnight, the two moments of Lanka-midnight are considered equal. Wise and learned scholars have previously performed the correction for **ascensional difference** <term>original: *cara-saṃskāra*; a correction that accounts for the variation in the length of the day due to the observer's latitude</term> before the time of midnight. 

This was stated by the venerable **Surya** <note>referring to the *Surya Siddhanta*, the authoritative text on Indian astronomy</note>. Because the means of achieving this calculation is mentioned here, and because it was not stated that it should be provided to others for the purpose of proof, the correction is not performed. 

Right here <note>original: *atraivātra*; a repetition in the manuscript (dittography)</note>, the **mean planet** <term>original: *madhyagraha*; the theoretical position of a planet assuming a perfectly circular and uniform orbit</term> produced from the **day-count** <term>original: *ahargaṇa*; the total number of days elapsed from the beginning of a cosmic era</term> exists at the time of Lanka-midnight. This is known through the true measure of the mean day-count. 

Subsequently, through the correction for the **rising difference**, the mean planet is established for the time of Lanka-midnight. At that very same time, the mean planet for one’s own local region is produced at midnight. Because of this, there is an absence of the correction for ascensional difference. 

Then, by applying the **longitudinal correction** <term>original: *deśāntara-saṃskāra*; a correction to account for the distance between the local meridian and the prime meridian of Lanka</term>, the position for local midnight is produced. From this mean position of one's own night, the mean planet for the local midnight is derived. 

This has also been said regarding the **true midnight** <note>original: *spaṣṭārdharātra*</note>. Therefore, by applying the correction of the **equation of center** <term>original: *bhujaphala*; the correction for the elliptical nature of an orbit</term> occurring in the interval, one finds the mean planet for the time of local true midnight. Finally, by applying the corrections for the **equations of apogee and conjunction** <term>original: *manda-śīghra-phala*</term>, the planet becomes not-yet-true <note>original: *aspaṣṭo*; literally "not clear." This may be a scribal error for *spaṣṭo* (true/clear), or refers to a specific intermediate stage of calculation</note> in this context.

By the venerable **Sun** <note>original: *Bhagavatā Sūryeṇa*; referring to the *Surya Siddhanta*, the authoritative text believed to be revealed by the Sun God</note>, the correction for **ascensional difference** <term>original: *cara-saṃskāra*; a correction for the variation in the length of the day based on local latitude</term> was brought forth through the sequence starting from the northern path. This should be understood by the wise through the successive planetary steps.

## Now, the Correction of the Sun

In this calculation, the **Sun** <term>original: *Ravi*; the mean position of the Sun</term> is at 1s 05° 01' 17". The **Apogee** <term>original: *mandocca*; the point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Earth</term> is at 2s 11° 15' 55". 

By subtracting the Sun's position from the Apogee, the **Mean Anomaly** <term>original: *manda-kendra*; the angular distance of a planet from its apogee</term> is produced: 2s 11° 04' 58". From this, following the previously stated rules, the **Sine of the anomaly** <term>original: *bhujajyā*</term> is 13° 06' 52". 

This is multiplied by the **True Circumference** <term>original: *spaṣṭa-paridhi*; the corrected circumference of the epicycle</term> of 13° 51', resulting in 31 3 4 5 7. When this product is divided by the 360 degrees of the **Zodiacal Circle** <term>original: *bhagaṇāṃśa*</term>, the result is 82 15. 

From this, the arc-conversion produces the **Equation of the Center** <term>original: *manda-phala*; the correction required to find the true position from the mean position</term> in minutes: 82' 31". When this is added or subtracted <note>the text specifies "dhana" (addition) or "ṛṇa" (subtraction) based on the quadrant</note> to the mean position, the **True Sun** <term>original: *spaṣṭa-ravi*</term> is found to be:
2s 13° 35' 56".

## Now, the Correction of the Current Daily Motion

Regarding the rule "multiply by the difference of sines":
The **Mean Motion** <term>original: *madhyama-gati*; the average daily speed</term> of the Sun is 59' 08". The difference between the tabular segments for the Sun's **True Sine** is 26 5. 

The **Daily Motion** <term>original: *bhukti*</term> of 56' 21" is multiplied by this and then divided by 225 <note>a standard divisor in Indian trigonometry used for sine table intervals</note>, resulting in 53' 06". This is then multiplied by the **True Circumference** of 13° 51', giving 59 5 03. 

When divided by the 360 degrees of the circle, the resulting correction for the **Velocity** <term>original: *gati-phala*</term> is 13' 05". Because the anomaly is in the half of the orbit starting with Capricorn, this value is subtracted from the mean motion of 59' 08". Thus, the **True Motion of the Sun** is 57' 22" per day.

## Now, the Correction of the Moon

The **Moon** <term>original: *Candra*; the mean position</term> is at 1s 04° 13' 15"...

<meta>This page continues the mathematical operations for planetary positions. When the **Anomaly of Conjunction** <term>original: *śīghrakendra*; the angular distance of a planet from its conjunction with the Sun</term> is in the signs starting with Capricorn, the **cosine-correction** <term>original: *koṭiphala*</term> should be added to the **radius** <term>original: *trijyā*; the standard radius of the calculation circle</term>. When the Anomaly of Conjunction is in the signs starting with Cancer, the cosine-correction should be subtracted from the radius. To the square of this result, one should add the square of the **sine-correction** <note>original: *bhujaphala*</note> of the Anomaly of Conjunction. The square root of this sum is the **Hypotenuse** <term>original: *valakarṇa*; the distance from the center of the earth to the planet on its epicycle</term>.

**Now, the method for finding the Equation of Conjunction is stated:**

Multiply the sine-correction by the radius and divide by the hypotenuse. 53 The result, when converted from a value into an arc in minutes and so on, is the **Equation of Conjunction** <term>original: *śīghraphala*</term>. This is the concise method. When the sine-correction of the conjunction is multiplied by the radius and divided by the recently calculated hypotenuse, the result obtained is the Equation of Conjunction in minutes.

**Now, the application of these corrections to the planets is described:**

"This is applied to Mars and the other planets at the beginning and in the fourth operation." 54 This means the Equation of Conjunction should be applied to the positions of Mars and the other planets <note>original: *bhaumādī*; refers to the five planets: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note> during the first step and the fourth step of the calculation process.

**Now, the sequence of the correction process is stated:**

"For the Sun and the Moon, there is one correction of the Center; for Mars and the others, it is said: Center, then Center, then Center again, and then Conjunction, in that order." 55 

This means that for the Sun and the Moon, only one **Equation of the Center** <term>original: *manda-karman*; the correction for the planet's elliptical orbit</term> needs to be applied to find their true position. However, for Mars and the other planets, the method of refinement is now explained: first the Conjunction, then the Center, then the Center again, and then the Conjunction...

**The end of the Vikram order 45: Statement of the specific rules for producing the results.**

"Apply half of the **Equation of Conjunction** <term>original: *śīghraphala*; the correction that accounts for the Earth's own motion around the Sun</term> in the middle, and then the whole desired value." 46

First, half of the Equation of Conjunction should be applied to the **Mean Planet** <term>original: *madhyamagraha*; the average position of a planet as if it moved in a perfect circle</term>. Then, half of the calculated **Equation of Center** <term>original: *mandaphala*; the correction for the planet's elliptical orbit</term> should be applied to that position which has already been adjusted by half of the Equation of Conjunction.

Then, the full calculated Equation of Center should be applied to the Mean Planet; this becomes the **Manda-corrected position**. Finally, the full calculated Equation of Conjunction should be applied to that Manda-corrected position.

That result is the **True Planet** <term>original: *spaṣṭagraha*; the actual position of the planet in the sky as seen by an observer</term>. 46

**Now, on the Clarification of Velocity:**

In this section, the specific rules for the observation-based adjustments are first stated:

"The **True Daily Motion** <term>original: *spaṣṭabhukti*; the actual speed at which a planet moves across the sky in a 24-hour period</term> is determined from the **Mean Daily Motion** <term>original: *madhyamabhukti*</term> by adding or subtracting the minutes of arc calculated from the **Sine-Difference** <term>original: *dojyāntara*; the difference between two consecutive sine values used to find the rate of change</term> and other factors." 47

In an expert calculation, the Mean Daily Motion is the base. For the Moon, the True Daily Motion is determined from the Equation of Center; the remaining velocity is found by the same method using the Sine-Difference. The Mean Daily Motion is multiplied by the Sine-Difference. The resulting minutes of arc should then be added to or subtracted from the Moon's Mean Daily Motion according to the current calculation method.

**The clarification of velocity is described in four verses:**

"The correction to the planet's daily motion should be performed just like the correction for the Equation of Center. The daily motion is multiplied by the Sine-Difference..." 48

The minutes of the **Manda Epicycle** <term>original: *mandaparidhi*; the small circle used to model the planet's elliptical path</term> and the **Revolutions** <term>original: *bhagaṇa*; the number of full orbits a planet completes in a specific period</term> are used to find the minutes of arc...

<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical instructions for planetary astronomy, specifically shifting from calculating a planet’s corrected position (longitude) to its true daily velocity (motion). Both these operations should be performed; in the signs beginning with Capricorn <term>original: *makarādau*; the point where the correction changes sign</term>, the value is negative (subtraction), and in those beginning with Aries, it is positive (addition).

The clarified **Daily Motion** <term>original: *bhukti*; the distance a planet travels in one day</term> is thus declared by the illustrious **Son of Jishnu** <note>original: *śrī joṣṇubhunita*; referring to the great astronomer Brahmagupta (son of Jishnu), author of the *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta*</note>.

In that calculation, by the difference of the two, the radius is multiplied by the final **Hypotenuse** <term>original: *karṇa*; here, the distance from the Earth to the planet</term>... 50. When the **Variable Hypotenuse** <term>original: *cala-karṇa*</term> is divided, if the hypotenuse is greater than the radius, the result is added; if the radius is greater, it is subtracted from the motion. Through this subtraction, **Retrograde Motion** <term>original: *vakra gati*; the appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky</term> occurs. 50

Regarding the **Equation of Center Correction** <term>original: *mandakarma*; the adjustment for the planet's elliptical orbit</term>: from the mean motion of the planet, one must bring about the result of the planet’s daily motion. Just as the Equation of Center is calculated for the position, so too must the adjustment for the motion be calculated. Where the center is at the peak or the base (perigee/apogee), there is no change in motion. Therefore, the planet's motion is multiplied by the difference in the **Sines** <term>original: *dorjyā*; the sine of the anomaly</term>...

This should then be multiplied by the planet's own circumference and divided by the number of **Revolutions** <term>original: *bhagaṇa*; a full cycle of the planet through the zodiac</term>. The resulting minutes of arc, when applied to the **Mean Motion** <term>original: *madhyama gati*</term>, results in the negative or positive adjustment in the signs starting with Capricorn. This produces the **Manda-Corrected Velocity** <term>original: *manda-spaṣṭa-gati*</term>.

Next, to find the **Anomaly of Conjunction Velocity** <term>original: *śīghra-kendra-gati*</term>, one must subtract the planet's motion from the Sun's motion. Using the radius and the hypotenuse—where the radius is well-known—the final calculation is performed. Multiply by the distance between the Sun and the planet, and divide by the variable factor. The resulting velocity is the **Equation of Conjunction result** <term>original: *śīghraphala*</term>.

This should be applied to the Manda-corrected motion. If the hypotenuse is greater than the radius, then at that time, if the result is greater than the motion and requires subtraction, **Retrograde Motion** <term>original: *vakra gati*</term> occurs. This is the meaning.

The term **Deflection** <term>original: *valana*; the transformation of coordinates between the ecliptic and the equator</term> is used alongside the word for radius...

### Example

First, in the process of clarifying the position of **Mars** <term>original: *bhauma*</term>:

The **Mean Mars** <term>original: *madhyamo bhauma*; the average position of the planet before corrections</term> is 5 [signs] 25° 56' 53". Its **Mean Sun** <term>original: *madhyārka*; here functioning as the Shighra or "fast" point</term> is 1 [sign] 05° 01' 13". Because this falls in the second quadrant, its **Base Arc** <term>original: *bhuja*; the distance to the nearest cardinal point on the circle</term> is 1 [sign] 25° 15' 05". Dividing this by the standard intervals, we obtain the **Sine Segment** <term>original: *jyākhaṇḍa*</term> of 3 4 05, with a remainder of 10 51. When this is multiplied by the difference between the current and next motion (22) it equals 23 55 50; then, divided by the appropriate divisor, we get 10 35. This value, added to the sine segment for the base arc, yields the **Sine of the Base** <term>original: *bhujajyā*</term> of 34 15 38.

Regarding the **Epicycles** <term>original: *paridhi*; the small circles used in ancient models to explain irregular planetary movement</term>: the **Even Shighra Epicycle** <term>original: *yugma śīghra paridhi*</term> is 235 and the **Odd Shighra Epicycle** <term>original: *oja śīghra paridhi*</term> is 232. Their difference is 3.

The Sine of the Base (34 15 38) is multiplied by this difference [3], resulting in 23 58 51. When divided by the **Radius** <term>original: *trijyā*; the standard radius used in calculations, often 3438 minutes of arc</term>, the result is 2 54. Subtracting this small amount from the base epicycle of 235, the **Corrected Epicycle** <term>original: *spaṣṭā-paridhi*</term> becomes 222.

By multiplying the Sine of the Base (34 15 38) by this corrected epicycle and dividing by the **360 degrees of the circle** <term>original: *bhagaṇāṃśaiḥ*</term>, we obtain the **Equation of Sine** <term>original: *bhujajyā-phala*</term>: 210 3 55.

With the **slow true motion** <term>manda-spaṣṭa-gati; the velocity of a planet corrected for its elliptical orbit</term> of **24 38**, and the motion **23 55 58**, when divided by the divisors, the obtained minutes of motion etc. are **6 30**. This is the **slow anomaly** <term>manda-kendra; the angular distance from the planet's apogee</term>. Because it begins from Aries, having reached **31 16**, the addition results in a **slow true motion** <note>original: *meda-spaṣṭā-gati*</note> of **31 56**.

This value is subtracted from the **fast motion** <term>śīghra-bhukti; the motion of the planet's fast-moving reference point, related to the Earth's orbit</term> of **55 8**, resulting in the **velocity of the fast anomaly** <term>śīghra-kendra-gati</term> of **11 12 15**. The **Radius** <term>trijyā; the standard radius of the calculation circle</term> is **34 38**. In the calculation for the other **fast correction** <term>śīghraphala; the second major correction in Indian astronomy</term>, the **Hypotenuse** <term>karṇa; the distance from the Earth to the planet</term> is **35 52 01**. 

By the difference of these two, **5 14 01**, multiplied, the result is **108 55 26**. Divided by this **mobile hypotenuse** <note>original: *cala-karṇa*</note> **35 52**, the quotient obtained is **23 55**. This leading hypotenuse is greater than the Radius; therefore, for the purpose of the minutes of the motion result, it is added. By **2 55**, the **slow motion** <note>original: *meda-gati*</note> **30 56** is corrected, and the **True Motion of Mars** <note>original: *bhīma-spaṣṭā gati*</note> becomes **40 51**.

## Regarding the True Position of Mercury

In that calculation, the **mean slow motion** <term>madhyama-manda-gati</term> is in **Taurus** <note>original: *vṛṣabha*</note> at **1 05 53 23**. Its **fast point** <term>śīghra</term> is **9 8 26 5 18**. Having subtracted this, the **fast anomaly** <term>śīghra-kendra</term> obtained is **12 21 45**. Its **base** <term>bhuja; the side of the triangle used to calculate the sine</term> is **12 21 45**. Its **arc-minutes** <term>liptā</term> are **306 1 45**. In the sum of the three **sine-segments** <term>jyāpiṇḍa; pre-calculated values used to derive the sine of an angle</term> of **1585**, by the subsequent difference of **143 minutes**, the remaining **136 45** is multiplied to get **156 4 43**. Dividing that result, the quotient obtained is **89 51**.

### According to the Method of Ganesha

Divided by the fractional part of the circle, the resulting difference in the **Equation of Motion** <note>original: "gati-phala-bhede"</note> in minutes is 5 [and] 25. # 55. The True Motion of Planets and the Civil Day

-> **True Motion and the Civil Day** <-

The **true motion of the planet** <term>graha-spaṣṭa-gati: the actual daily speed of a planet as seen from Earth, which varies based on its elliptical orbit</term> should be multiplied by the measures of the planet's rising. This is performed using the "thirty-three" <note>khāgni: literally 'sky-fire' representing 30 in the Katapayadi system, but here likely referring to the 30 degrees of a sign</note> or the units of the current sign. This is combined with the **units of respiration** <term>vakra-asu: a unit of time roughly equal to 4 seconds, the duration of one breath</term> in the calculation of the **day-night period** <term>ahorātra: a full nycthemeron or 24-hour cycle</term>. 

For a planet whose position has been corrected by **precessional degrees** <term>sāyana: 'with precession', referring to the tropical longitude used to find rising times</term>, identify the current zodiac sign. Multiply the planet's true motion—expressed in minutes and so on—by the **equatorial rising time** <term>laṅkodaya-asu: the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise at the Earth's equator</term> of that current sign. Divide this product by 1800 <note>the number of minutes in a single 30-degree zodiac sign</note>. 

The resulting **time units** <note>original: "asu"</note> should be added to or subtracted from the standard 21,600 units <note>the number of 'asu' in 60 ghaṭīs or 24 hours</note>. However, the text here specifies a base of 21,400 <note>representing a sidereal day or a specific calculation constant</note>. This defines the planet’s **civil day units** <note>original: "ahorātrāsava"</note>. 

### Example:
The **true motion** <note>spaṣṭa-gati</note> is 11; 4, 25, 55. 
The **tropical position** <note>sāyana</note> is 23; 12, 33. 
The measure of rising for the sign of **Taurus** <note>vṛṣabha</note> in minutes is <unclear>253</unclear>, which when multiplied yields 1518 <note>the duration of Taurus's rising in 'asu'</note>. 

Using this, the **Sun's true motion** is 57' 29". 
Multiplied [by 1518], the product is 87255; 52. 
Divided by 1800, the result is 48; 18. 
This is added to the base units of 21400. 
The resulting **civil day units for the Sun** are 21558; 28.

Now, concerning the **declination** <note>krānti</note> combined with the rising... <note>The text here becomes difficult to decipher due to the dark smudge on line 15</note> ...otherwise, half the day... 80...

# 51. Calculation of Declination and the Diurnal Circle

[...] the **sine of declination** <term>krāntijyā: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator, expressed as a sine value</term>. [3]

When the **versine of declination** <term>utkramajyā: the 'reversed sine' or versine (1 - cosine) of the declination angle</term> is subtracted from the **radius** <term>vyāsadala: literally 'half-diameter', the standard radius of 3438 minutes used in Indian trigonometry</term>, the remainder is the **radius of the diurnal circle** <term>ahorātra-vṛtta-vyāsadala: the radius of the circle upon which a planet travels during its 24-hour rotation</term>.

This is the intended meaning. Specifically, regarding the **variation in the diurnal circle** <term>dina-vyāsa-bheda: the change in the diameter of the day-circle based on the planet's latitude</term>, if the declination is southern, it is situated in the southern direction; if northern, then in the northern direction. We shall now see this in a **worked example** <term>udāharaṇa: a mathematical demonstration</term>.

-> **Mathematical Example** <-

The **tropical Sun** <term>sāyana-sūrya: the longitude of the Sun adjusted for the precession of the equinoxes</term> is at 2 signs, 23 degrees, 18 minutes, and 33 seconds <note>2s 23° 18' 33" or approximately 83° 18'</note>. From this, the **sine of declination** <note>original: "krāntijyā"</note> is calculated as 23, 55, and 43. The **arc** <term>dhanu: the angle corresponding to a sine value</term> produced from this is 150 degrees and 55 minutes.

In the process of finding the sine of declination, the primary **sine of declination** <note>original: "krāntijyā"</note> is 11, 55, and 43. To calculate the **versine of declination** <note>original: "krāntijyā-utkramajyā"</note>, we take the arc minutes of 150, 55. Using the standard **sine-table interval** <term>पिण्ड (piṇḍa): the 24 segments of 225 minutes each used to calculate sines</term> of 225, the **accumulated versine** <note>original: "utkramajyā-piṇḍa"</note> is found. After subtracting the remainder of 25 minutes from 181, we obtain 15, 54. 

Dividing by the interval of 225, the quotient is 5, 132. Subtracting this from the **previous versine total** <note>original: "gata-utkramajyā-piṇḍa"</note> of 118, the **total versine** <note>original: "utkramajyā"</note> is 187, 22. 

When this versine of 187 is subtracted from the **total radius** <term>trijyā: the standard radius of the celestial sphere, usually 3438 minutes</term> of 3438, the resulting **radius of the diurnal circle** <note>original: "ahorātra-vyāsadalam"</note> for the northern declination is 3250, 16. Because the declination is northern, this value is applied to the north-south calculation.

-> **Calculation of Ascensional Difference** <-

Now we begin the **calculation of ascensional difference** <term>cara-sādhana: finding the difference between the local time of sunrise and the equatorial time of sunrise</term>.

The text now explains the division of day and night: 
The **sine of declination** <note>original: "krāntijyā"</note> is multiplied by the **sine of the equinoctial shadow** <term>viṣuvaj-jyā: a value representing the observer's latitude</term> and then multiplied by the **radius** <note>original: "trijyā"</note>. This product is then divided by the **radius of the diurnal circle** <note>original: "ahorātra-ardha-karṇa"</note>. The result is known as the **ascensional difference** <term>cara: the time added to or subtracted from 12 hours to find the length of the day</term>. [51]

If the declination is northern, this value is added to or subtracted from the respective periods of day and night according to the specific ritual or astronomical requirement.

From that arc, the **sine** <note>original: "jyā"</note> of the planet's position is found. That **equinoctial circle** <term>viṣuva-valaya: the celestial equator</term> relates to the Sun when it is at the beginning of **Aries or Libra** <term>meṣa-tulādi: the tropical equinox points where day and night are equal</term>. When subtracted or added, the results are the halves of the day and night. In the southern direction, this is reversed. How are the halves of the night and day derived? This refers to the **half-transit** <note>original: "dvādaśārdha saṅkrānti"</note>.

The sine, the **earth-sine** <term>kujyā: a linear distance related to the difference between the local and equatorial horizons</term>, and the sine of latitude are multiplied by the radius of the diurnal circle and the hypotenuse. This radius of the diurnal circle is then divided; the result is the **sine of the ascensional difference** <term>carajyā</term>. From that sine, the arc should be calculated. From that arc, the **ascensional breaths** <term>carāsava: units of time where 6 breaths equal 1 sidereal minute</term> are produced. 

This means the result is in the form of **breaths** <term>asu: a unit of time equivalent to 4 seconds</term>. The ascensional difference for the northern direction is calculated separately in its own place. On the diurnal circle, this should be subtracted or added. When combined with another sign or subtracted, the halves of the day and night are produced in sequence. This is the reversal through practice. When doubled, the full day and night durations are stated; from that, the half-day is produced, and from that, the half-night.

### The Fivefold Calculation

Now, he explains the fivefold calculation. Among them, he first describes the method for calculating the **zenith distance** <term>nata: the angular distance of a celestial body from the observer's zenith</term> of a planet.

> The minutes of the star-measure... for the **lunar days** <term>tithi</term>... the planet's minutes divided by the motion of the star... the measure is given in stars, signs, and so on. (Verse 25)

The minutes are measured as 800 <note>A single Nakshatra or lunar mansion spans exactly 800 minutes of arc, or 13°20'</note>. The **elapsed motion** <term>bhoga</term> is 800 minutes, which is equal to the motion of the planet; this is the meaning of the verse. In the context of the lunar day, it refers to the elapsed motion of the lunar day... measured by the three worlds <note>original: "trailokya-mita," likely a poetic way to refer to a specific numerical value or the entirety of the calculation</term>.

By these [values], what is the result? The remaining times should be divided by the motion-times. From the resulting quotient, the days and other units are produced. If the portion yet to be traversed <term>bhogya: the remaining part of a celestial division to be covered by a planet</term> is required, then that same remainder should be subtracted from the total measure <term>bhabhoga: the full longitudinal span of a nakshatra (800 minutes) or a zodiac sign</term>. ### Now he describes the calculation of the Yogas

The sum of the minutes <note>original: "limpā", a synonym for kalā or minutes of arc</note> of the Sun and Moon is divided by the total measure of the **Yoga** <term>yoga: an astrological period defined by the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon; there are 27 yogas in total</term>. The past and future portions, multiplied by sixty [60] and divided by the total measure of the yoga, result in the time elapsed or remaining in **nāḍīs** <term>nāḍī: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes, also called a ghaṭikā</term> and its subdivisions.

The minutes of the sum of the Sun and Moon, divided by the total span of the **asterism** <term>nakshatra: a lunar mansion</term>, result in the elapsed or future ghaṭikās. By the measure of the traverse <note>original: "bhoga"</note>, or by the measure of the **lunar day** <term>tithi</term>, the values are divided by twenty-one [21] <note>likely referring to a specific constant or divisor in this specific calculation</note>. By this division, one knows the knowledge of the "mountains" <note>original: "śaila", a numerical code (bhūta-saṃkhyā) for the number 7</note> regarding the traversed portion.

### On the calculation of the Lunar Day (Tithi)

Subtract the minutes of the Sun from those of the Moon. This difference is divided by the measure of the **Tithi** <term>tithi: a lunar day, defined as the time it takes for the longitudinal gap between the Moon and Sun to increase by 12 degrees</term> to find the past and future portions. These are then multiplied by sixty [60] and divided by the daily motion to yield the time in nāḍīs and seconds.

From the minutes of the Sun and Moon, divided by the measure of the lunar day, the elapsed tithis are found. Here too, just as with the traversed portion, the portion to be traversed is multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in their daily motions; thus the nāḍīs are obtained.

### Example

**True Sun:** 5 [signs] 3 [degrees] 5 [minutes] 49 [seconds]
**True Motion:** 57 [minutes] 21 [seconds]
**True Moon:** 7 [signs] 7 [degrees] 11 [minutes] 33 [seconds]
**Motion:** 803 [minutes] 12 [seconds]
**The Moon minus the Sun:** 5 [signs] 10 [degrees] 35 [minutes] 57 [seconds]
**Elapsed time (in minutes):** 10835 [minutes] 57 [seconds]
**Divided by the measure of a lunar day (720):** the quotient is the elapsed lunar days. <note>In Indian astronomy, a Tithi is exactly 720 minutes of arc (12 degrees) of separation between the Sun and Moon</note>

Dividing by the extent of 800, the obtained **elapsed yoga** is the 18th **Nakshatra-Yoga** <term>yoga: one of 27 astrological divisions based on the combined longitude of the Sun and Moon</term>. Dividing by the **combined motion** <term>gati-yoga: the sum of the daily motions of the Sun and Moon</term> of 895 | 31 | 53, the initial ghaṭikās of the Yoga are 53 | 40.

...the **Fixed Karanas** <term>sthira-karaṇa: four specific half-lunar days that occur only once a month at specific times</term> are **Śakuni**, **Catuṣpada**, **Nāga**, and **Kiṃstughna**. 

### On the Fixed and Mobile Karanas

The second half of the fourteenth day of the **dark fortnight** <note>original: "kṛṣṇāyāś-caturdaśyaḥ"</note>, both halves of the fifteenth day <note>the New Moon or Amavasya</note>, and the first half of the first day of the **bright fortnight** <note>Shukla Pratipada</note> are designated as the fixed ones. Specifically, the second half of the fourteenth is **Śakuni** <note>literally "The Bird"</note>; the first and second halves of the fifteenth are **Catuṣpada** <note>"The Quadruped"</note> and **Nāga** <note>"The Serpent"</note> respectively; and the first half of the following bright first day is **Kiṃstughna**. 87

Next, the **Mobile Karanas** <term>cara-karaṇa: the seven repeating half-lunar days</term> are described: 

The seven karanas beginning with **Bava** occur in a repeating cycle throughout the month. 88 These seven are: **Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇija,** and **Viṣṭi**.

<margin>8 |</margin> These seven mobile karanas rotate eight times throughout the lunar month. This means that from the second half of the first day of the bright fortnight, these karanas cycle repeatedly until the first half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. 

### Conclusion of the Chapter on True Motion

One should calculate the duration of these karanas based on the **half-duration of a tithi** <term>tithy-ardha: the time it takes for the lunar day to reach its midpoint</term>. 

This concludes the description of the **true motion** <term>spaṣṭagati: the mathematically corrected position of a planet as seen from Earth</term> of the Sun and the other planets according to their own movements. 89 

For each of the seven mobile karanas, their "enjoyment" or duration is exactly half of a lunar day. This time of half a tithi must be carefully determined. In this manner, the true motion of the Sun and other planets—which is the very form of correct astronomical action for the benefit of men—has been spoken by me. 

**Thus ends the Chapter on True Motion.**

The *Grahalaghava-Prakashika* <note>The "Light on the Grahalaghava"</note> composed by **Vishvanatha** is now complete regarding this second house of calculations, the Chapter on True Motion.

## Now begins the Chapter on the Three Problems
### In the Commentary

In this section, the author explains the **knowledge of directions** <term>dik-jñāna: the method for orienting oneself to the cardinal points</term> through four verses:

On a stone surface, or on smooth, clean earth, or perhaps on a surface prepared with **Vajralepa** <term>vajralepa: an ancient Indian "hard-plaster" or cement made of organic materials like resin and clay</term>, one should draw a **perfect circle** <term>sama-maṇḍala</term> using a piece of chalk. 1

In the center of that circle, one should place a **gnomon** <term>śaṅku: a vertical rod used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurements</term> designed to be **twelve digits** <note>original: "dvādaśāṅgula"; a standard measurement in ancient Indian astronomy</note> in height. Mark two points where the tip of its shadow touches the circle in the forenoon and the afternoon. 2

Having marked those two points at the intersections of the circle, a line should be drawn between them to establish the **North-South** direction. 3

Between the points of the North and South directions, a **West** (and East) direction line is created. These are determined by the use of **fishes** <note>original: "matsyaiḥ"; this refers to the fish-shaped intersection of two circular arcs used in geometry to draw perpendicular lines</note>. The **intermediate directions** <note>North-East, South-East, etc.</note> are determined in the same manner. 4

### Commentary on the Methods

Regarding the determination of directions: first, the surface must be soft and clean, or a stone surface made perfectly level. When preparing the surface with plaster, its levelness should be tested using the "water-level" method <note>checking if water sits still on the surface</note>. This is the intended meaning of "on a stone surface, a circle is drawn."

Alternatively, if a stone surface is unavailable, one uses a ground prepared with clay or **Vajralepa** <note>hard cement</note> that has been made perfectly level. There, a gnomon of the desired height—usually twelve digits—is placed. In the middle of the circle, where the center is established, the lines should be drawn according to the prescribed method.

Then, at that spot, having placed the twelve-digit gnomon on the level surface so its head is perfectly vertical, one observes the shadow...

# The Division of the East and West Directions and the Placement of the Gnomon
In the division where the tip of the shadow touches the circumference of that circle: in the forenoon <insert>----</insert> until it enters [the circle], and in the afternoon as it exits [the circle]. At the points of both the entrance and the exit, one should mark them in order on the ground.

## Calculation of the Shadow’s Hypotenuse
Now, the method for knowing the **hypotenuse** <term>karṇa: the diagonal line connecting the top of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</term> of the shadow is stated:
The square of the **gnomon** <term>śaṅku: the vertical pillar</term> added to the square of the shadow, and the square root of that sum, is called the square of the hypotenuse. From the square root of the sum of the squares of the gnomon and the shadow, the hypotenuse is found. Conversely, the shadow is found from the gnomon. From the sum of the squares of a **twelve-digit gnomon** <note>original: "dvādaśāṅgula-śaṅku"</note> and its shadow, the square root provides the **hypotenuse of the desired shadow** <note>original: "iṣṭacchāyā-karṇa"</note>.

### Example
In this case, on that very same day, the shadow measures 10 digits.
The gnomon is 12; its **square** <term>varga</term> is 144.
The shadow is 10; its square is 100.
The sum of these two is 244.
From this, the square root—which is the desired shadow-hypotenuse—is 15 | 37 <note>The value is expressed in sexagesimal notation, roughly 15.62</note>.
The square of this is 244.
If the **square of the hypotenuse** <note>original: "śru-varga"</note> is 244 and 100 is subtracted from it, the square root of the remainder gives the shadow as 10.
In the reverse case for the gnomon:
From the square of the hypotenuse, 244, subtract the square of the shadow, 100.
The remainder is 144.
The square root of this is known to be the gnomon: 12.
Now, the calculation for the knowledge of the solar declination is explained:

---

> The sum of the three sines <note>original: "triguṇa"</note> and the Sun's **declination** <term>apakrama: the angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator</term>... divided by the terrestrial sine... from the heap of days...
> Then, having subtracted twelve... called the **solstice** <term>ayana</term>.
> From that, the desired base and the half-square of the shadow...
> Thus... regarding the Sun’s position in the signs...

# Calculation of the Precession of the Equinoxes

In a **Great Age** <term>mahayūga: a vast cycle of 4,320,000 years</term>, the division of the era involves a cycle that completes six hundred times. This means that within this period, there are six hundred revolutions <note>original: "ṣat śatam"</note>. 

By using the **count of days** <term>yu-gaṇa: the total number of days elapsed since the start of the current epoch</term>, one should multiply by six hundred and divide by the total number of terrestrial days in an era. Through this process, one obtains the **revolutions** <term>bhagaṇa: completed orbital cycles</term>. These completed revolutions are to be discarded; from the remainder, which represents the current position in fractions of a cycle, the degrees and minutes are calculated. 

## Determining the Precession Angle
One must then determine the **precession** <term>ayana: the shifting of the equinoxes and solstices</term>. Divide the result by three and then by ten <note>This describes a mathematical process to find the Ayanāṃśa, which in this system oscillates within a specific range</note> to obtain the **precession degrees** <term>ayanāṃśa: the arc between the fixed start of the zodiac and the moving equinox</term>. From these degrees, the **declination shadow** <term>krānti-chāyā</term> and related values are determined, based on the calculation of the day.

### Direct Observation and Proof
An example of this has been shown. Now, the **direct proof** <term>pratyakṣa-pramāṇa</term> of the stated position is given:

When the equinoxes and the two solstices move in the **circle of the constellations** <note>original: "cakra"</note>, and the shadow changes due to this motion, the **two equinoxes** <term>viṣuvat-dvaya</term> and the **solstices** <term>ayana</term> move eastward. This shift causes a difference in the shadow. 

When the sun moves toward the northern or southern solstices or reaches the two equinoxes, the **true observed** <term>sphuṭa-pratyakṣa</term> position may appear shifted to the south or north. This shift is visible. Now, if one asks whether this movement is entirely westward or otherwise, it is said:

It is "Eastward." It should be understood that the movement is toward the east. The **reduced shadow** <term>chāyā-kona</term> of the **mean sun** <note>the sun's position calculated as if it moved at a constant speed</note> should be calculated according to the method to be described.

# Refining the Sun’s Position and the Shadow

The position of the **True Sun** <term>spashṭa-sūrya: the actual observed position of the sun, corrected from its mean position</term> is calculated through these three methods. When that value is adjusted—either by subtraction or addition—this represents the Sun’s position relative to the first sign of the zodiac <note>Aries</note>. It should be understood that as the Sun moves along the **ecliptic** <term>krānti-vṛtta: the sun's apparent path in the sky</term>, the calculations shift according to the specific signs. If the remainder of the Sun’s position exceeds the current sign, one must calculate the movement through the next signs using the inverse method of revolving the arc.

## Determining the Equinoctial Shadow

Now, the author explains the calculation of the **equinoctial shadow** <term>aksha-prabhā or vishuvan-prabhā</term>. 

The shadow cast in one’s own locality <term>svadeśa</term> at the exact time of the equinox—whether it falls to the south or the north—is known as the equinoctial shadow. In any specific place, this is measured using a **standard gnomon of twelve digits** <term>dvādaśāṅgula-śaṅku: a vertical pillar or rod used to measure time and latitude</term>. The midday shadow of this gnomon, when the sun is at the celestial equator, determines the specific **latitude** <term>aksha</term> of that desired region.

### Illustrative Example: Varanasi
In this calculation, for the city of **Kashi** <note>the sacred city of Varanasi</note>, the equinoctial shadow is determined to be:
**5 digits and 45 minutes** <note>original: 5 | 45 | 12, where 12 represents the height of the gnomon</note>.

## Calculation of Latitude and Colatitude

Now, we proceed to find the **colatitude** <term>lamba</term> and the **latitude** <term>aksha</term>. 

The formula is as follows: The shadow of the gnomon is multiplied by the **radius** <term>trijyā: the sine of the radius of the celestial sphere, often calculated as 3438</term> and then divided by the **equinoctial hypotenuse** <term>vishuvan-karṇa: the diagonal distance from the top of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</term>. 

To find these two values (latitude and colatitude):
1. Place the **radius** in two separate positions.
2. In one position, multiply it by **twelve** <note>the height of the gnomon</note>.
3. In the other, multiply it by the **equinoctial shadow** <term>vishuvan-prabhā</term> calculated for that region.
4. Divide both resulting sums by the **equinoctial hypotenuse**.

The resulting arcs <note>the inverse sine of the results</note> will always give the **colatitude** and the **latitude** respectively for the two hemispheres, usually pointing in the southern direction in these calculations.

### Numerical Example
The **radius** is 3438.
This is multiplied by the **gnomon** (12), which equals 41,256... <note>The text continues with the multiplication 12 * 40 in the final line, likely leading into the next step of the calculation</note>.

## Midday Calculations and the Zenith Distance

Now, the author speaks on the knowledge of the **Sine of the Zenith Distance** <term>natanyā</term> and the **Sine of Altitude** <term>koṭijyā</term> at midday. He says: "If the direction [of the latitude and declination] is the same, find their difference; otherwise, find their sum."

To find the Sun's **zenith distance** <term>nata-āṃśa: the angular distance from the point directly overhead to the object</term>, one must consider the **declination** <term>apakrama: the angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator</term>. If the latitude and the declination are in the same direction, subtract one from the other. If they are in opposite directions, their sum should be taken. The result is the zenith distance of the Sun.

From this zenith distance, the **Sine of the Zenith Distance** <term>bhujajyā</term> is calculated. To find the **Sine of Altitude** <term>unnatāṃśa-jyā</term>, subtract the zenith distance from ninety degrees and find the sine of the remainder.

### A Practical Example
In this example, at 45;31 ghatis <note>a unit of time where 60 ghatis equal 24 hours</note> of the elapsed day, the position of the Sun at midday is 11 signs, 5 degrees, 51 minutes, and 25 seconds. When adjusted for **precession** <term>sāyana: the tropical longitude, which includes the shifting of the equinoxes</term>, the position is 2 signs, 13 degrees, 2 minutes, and 11 seconds.

The sine of this position <term>bhujajyā</term> is 13;3;2. This is multiplied by the **Sine of Maximum Declination** <term>parama-apakrama-jyā: the sine of the angle of the Earth's axial tilt, roughly 24 degrees in ancient Indian systems</term>, which is 13;10. The result is 181;8;54;35. When divided by the **Radius** 34;38, the result is the **Sine of Declination** <term>krāntijyā</term> of 110;35. From this, the **minutes of declination** <term>krānti-kalā</term> are found to be 11;2 through multiplication and division.

Having taken the remainder of the sine as stated, by the square root of the **Cosine of Latitude** <term>lambajyā: the sine of the co-latitude (90° minus latitude)</term> and the **Tangent of the Latitude** multiplied by the **Sun** <note>original: "arka" — in astronomical mathematics, "Sun" often stands for the number 12, the standard height of the gnomon in digits</note>, then divided by the Cosine of Latitude, the result is the **Equinoctial Shadow** <term>viṣuvaj-jāpalabhā: the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</term>.

**In the example:**
The Latitude Minutes are 15;35;55.
The **Sine of the Latitude** <note>original: "asojyā" probably for "akṣajyā"</note> is 15;82;55.
The square of this is 2300;55;2;55. 
Subtracting this very value from the **Square of the Radius** <term>trijyā-varga</term> (which is 15;55;18;55) <note>These values appear to be in a specific sexagesimal fractional notation used in medieval Indian Siddhantic tables</note>, the remainder is 55;55;227;55. 
The square root of this is the **Cosine of Latitude** <term>lambajyā</term>: 2102;25. 
The **Sine of the Latitude** <note>original: "antajyā" for "akṣajyā"</note> is 15;82;27. 
Multiplied by the **Sun** (12), it becomes 19801;25. 
Divided by the Cosine of Latitude (2102;25), the quotient is the **Equinoctial Shadow**: 
**5;45**.

When the **Reverse Procedure** <term>viloma-vidhi</term> is performed:
From the degrees of the observed shadow, the Sun is determined through its **Declination** <term>krānti</term>. Regarding this, he speaks a verse and a half on the calculation of the Sun:

->**Your own solar zenith distance degrees are subtracted from the direction if they are the same (South or North), and otherwise (if directions differ) they are added.**<-
->**From the remaining sine, multiplied by the radius and divided by the maximum declination sine, the arc is the Sun’s position beginning with Aries.**<-

**Explanation:**
"One's own" refers to the local observer. The "Solar zenith distance degrees" <term>arka-nata-bhāga</term> are the degrees the Sun is away from the point directly overhead at midday. If the direction of the shadow and the latitude are the same, they are subtracted; otherwise, their sum is taken. 

The result is the **Declination** <term>apakrama or krānti: the Sun's angular distance from the celestial equator</term>. Then, one should calculate the sine of this declination. Multiply it by the **Radius** <term>trijyā</term> and divide by the **Maximum Declination Sine** <term>parama-krāntijyā: usually the sine of 24 degrees</term>. The arc of the resulting value reveals the Sun's longitude starting from **Aries** <term>Meṣādi: the first sign of the zodiac</term>. If the result is within the first three signs (Aries, Taurus, Gemini), the Sun is...

# Calculation of the Sun

### Example

Let the **Mean Sun** <term>madhyama-ravi: the theoretical position of the sun if its motion were perfectly uniform</term> be 5 signs, 5°, 17', 7". 

The **Apogee** <term>manda-ucca: the point in the sun's orbit furthest from the earth</term> is 2 signs, 11°, 43', 55". 

By subtracting these, the **Anomaly** <term>manda-kendra: the angular distance of the sun from its apogee</term> is determined to be:
8 signs, 11°, 43', 32".

From this, the **Sine of the Arc** <term>bhujajyā</term> is 22; 10, 21. 

This value is multiplied by the difference of the odd and even quadrants <note>original: "ojayugmanereṇāntena"</note>, which is 7; 20. 
The product is 35; 43, 43. 
Divided by the **Radius** <term>trijyā</term>, the quotient is 0; 16. 

Using the desired **Even Circumference** <term>yugma-paridhi</term> of 24, the resulting **True Circumference** <term>spaṣṭa-paridhi</term> is 13; 47. 

By this, the **Sine of the Arc** (22; 10, 22) is multiplied, giving 3; 12, 35, 36. 
Dividing this by the **Degrees in a Circle** <term>bhagaṇāṃśa: 360 degrees</term>, the quotient is 84; 55. 

The arc of this value, which is the **Equation of Center** <term>manda-phala: the correction required to account for the sun's elliptical orbit</term> in minutes of arc <note>original: "kalātmakaṃ"</note>, is 84' 55".

Because the anomaly begins with the sign of **Aries** <term>meṣādi</term>, here, according to the **Inverse Method** <term>viloma-vidhi</term>, the negative or positive nature of the result is determined. The result is 1° 24' 55". 

Corrected by this value, the **True Sun** <term>spaṣṭo raviḥ</term> is 0 signs, 5°, 57', 17". 
The resulting **Mean Sun** <term>madhyamo raviḥ</term> is 2 signs, 3°, 10', 22".

From this, one should again calculate the **Equation of Center** and apply the **Iterative Correction** <term>asakṛt-saṃskāra-kriyayā: a repetitive mathematical process used to reach a stable, accurate value</term> to the previously derived Sun (0s 5° 57' 17") until the value becomes stable. 

Everything that has been said—referring to the rules like "in the rock, the fire, the arrow, the arrows" <note>original: "śilānaleumeṣu dām..." which likely refers to a numerical mnemonic or specific verse markers</note>—all of that has been demonstrated through the **Inverse Method**.

|| 28 ||

-> **Now, he brings forth the calculation for the Equinoctial Hypotenuse.** <-

**The Sine of Declination multiplied by the Equinoctial Hypotenuse, divided by the Sine of Latitude...** <note>This marks the beginning of a verse (v. 29) explaining the relationship between the sun's declination and the shadow's hypotenuse.</note>

The **Sine of Declination** <term>krāntijyā</term> is the Sine of the Sun’s Declination. By the wheel of the multipliers of the **Equinoctial Hypotenuse** <term>viṣuvat-karṇa</term>...

### Two Methods for Deriving the Hypotenuse
Now, for the **Calculation of the Hypotenuse** <term>karṇānayane</term> through two distinct methods, utilizing the Sines of the Latitude and Colatitude <note>original: "lambākṣa-jīve"</note>:

The **Equinoctial Shadow** <term>viṣuvacchāyā</term> multiplied by twelve and the **Sine of Declination** <term>krāntijyā</term> are used to determine the values for the **Prime Vertical** <term>samamaṇḍala: the great circle passing through the zenith and the east and west points of the horizon</term>.

By the **Sine of Colatitude** <note>original: "lambajyā"</note> and the others in sequence, the Equinoctial Shadow is multiplied by twelve. In both instances, when divided by the **Sine of Declination**, the **Hypotenuses of the Sun** located on the Prime Vertical are produced. In both cases, this result shall be the **Shadow-Hypotenuse** <term>karṇaḥ</term>.

### Example
30; 18, 5 multiplied by the **Equinoctial Shadow** <term>palabhayā</term> of 5; 45 equals 174; 18, 12, 56. When divided by the **Sine of Declination** of 11; 0, 3, 9, the obtained **Hypotenuse** is 17; 12.

Alternatively: 15; 45, 25 multiplied by twelve equals 189; 5, 0, 8. When divided by the **Sine of Declination** of 11; 0, 16, the obtained **Hypotenuse** is 17; 12. **|| 21 ||**

As far as the **Hypotenuse** <term>karṇa: the diagonal distance from the top of the gnomon to the tip of the shadow</term> and the mean distance are concerned: when the stated **Declination** <note>original: "krānti"; the angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator</note> is subtracted from the **Latitude** <term>akṣāṃśa</term> and the result is multiplied, then the calculation is purified. In that context, the **Mean Radius** <term>trijyā</term> is 3438. As it occurs, the mean movement is divided by the **Mean Solar Hypotenuse** <note>original: "madhyārka-karṇa"</note> to yield the **Resultant Hypotenuse** <term>phala-karṇa</term>.

**Example:**
Using the values 18; 55; 3 and the **Latitude** of 24; 48; 2. From the differences between these, the **Mean Solar Hypotenuse** is 2; 10; 5. This is multiplied by the **Equinoctial Shadow** <note>original: "palabhā"</note> of 32; 28 and the solar movement of 24. When divided, the **Resultant Hypotenuse** is 280; 20; 5. **|| 25 ||**

### Further derivation of the Sine of Amplitude

The **Sine of Declination** <term>krāntijyā</term> or the **Radius** <term>trijyā</term> is spoken of in relation to the **Sine of Colatitude** <term>lambajyā</term>. The **Sine of Amplitude** <note>original: "agrajyā"; the distance of the Sun at sunrise from the east point of the horizon</note> is multiplied by the **Hypotenuse of the Prime Vertical** <note>original: "samakarṇa"</note> and divided by the Radius to find the value in minutes and seconds.

Alternatively, the **Sine of Declination** of the desired planet is multiplied by its own **Desired Hypotenuse**, then multiplied by the **Mean Solar Hypotenuse** and divided by the Radius. The result is the Sine of Amplitude.

**Example:**
The **Sine of Declination** is 1120; 35 and the **Radius** is 3438. Multiplied by 28; 28, 54; 54; 54 and divided by the **Sine of Colatitude** of 1058; 5, the result for the **Sine of Amplitude** <note>original: "agrajyā"</note> is 2235; 54. This is then multiplied by the **Mean Solar Hypotenuse** value of 12; 5, resulting in 54852; 52. When divided by the Radius of 3438, the **Desired Sine of Amplitude** is 5; 55. **|| 26 ||**

<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical demonstrations of Indian astronomy, specifically focusing on the calculation of the gnomon's shadow. The previous page discussed the "Resultant Hypotenuse" and the "Sine of Amplitude." This section moves into the specific geometric derivation of the "surds" (square roots) used to determine the shadow's position in different hemispheres and directions.</meta>

The wise should take the result obtained—joined with half the square of the **gnomon** <term>śaṅku: a vertical pillar used to measure time and latitude by its shadow</term>—and divide it by the square of the **equinoctial shadow** <term>viṣuvadvarga/palabhā: the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term>. From the results obtained, known as the **surds** <term>karaṇī: in this context, the square of a quantity or a number whose square root is to be found</term>, the scholar should set them aside separately.

Then, the solar sine and the equinoctial shadow are multiplied by the multiplier. In the square root <note>original: "pada"</note> of the surd joined with that square, the result is added in the southern and northern **hemispheres** <term>gola</term> and the intermediate directions. Because the gnomon moves <note>original: "paribhramanti," describing the apparent motion of the Sun relative to the gnomon</note>, the gnomon in the northern hemisphere is said to be the square root of the difference of the squares.

### Detailed Calculation of the Surds

One should take half the square of the **Radius** <term>trijyā: the total sine of 3438 minutes used in Indian trigonometry</term> and diminish it by the square of the **Sine of ten degrees** <note>original: "daśajyā-varga"</note>. Multiply this by twelve, but take care not to multiply it by twelve a second time. 

Because the gnomon consists of twelve **digits** <term>aṅgula</term>, the mathematicians <note>original: "gaṇitavidbhiḥ"</note> should divide the result by the square of the **equinoctial shadow** <note>original: "palabhā"</note> joined with half the square of the gnomon. The quotient obtained from this is the "surd." This surd, or the group of surds, should be placed separately in a second position. 

Then, the solar sine multiplied by twelve is further multiplied by the multiplier obtained from the equinoctial shadow. Likewise, from the division by the square of the equinoctial shadow joined with half the square of the gnomon, the result is added to its own square. As the Sun rotates, the <insert>shadows</insert> <gloss>orderly</gloss> [move] in the southern and northern intermediate directions: the **South-West** <term>nairṛtya</term>, and the northern directions: **North-East** <term>īśāna</term> and **North-West** <term>vāyavya</term>. 

This means that in the first half of the day, the shadow moves from the **South-East** <term>āgneya</term> toward the North or South. In the second half of the day, it moves between the **South-West** and the **North-West**, following the southern or northern path. <unclear>si-ki-tta</unclear>

The square of the **Radius** <term>vijyā</term> is 13,518,855 <note>The text uses a slightly different value for the Radius square here compared to the start of the example</note>.
