For **Venus** <note>original: "bhṛgoḥ śukrasya"</note>, sixty is declared as the measure. These **diameters** <term>viṣkambhāḥ</term>, multiplied by **twice the radius** <term>dviguṇa-trijyā</term>, and joined with the **threefold hypotenuse** <note>original: "trivṛ-karṇa"</note>—in the **third operation** <term>tṛtīya-karmaņi</term>, in that threefold operation, the two **hypotenuses** <term>karṇau</term>, namely the **slow hypotenuse** <term>mandakarṇa</term> and the **fast hypotenuse** <term>śīghrakarṇa</term>—when divided by the sum of those two, they become the **true obtained hypotenuse** <term>spaṣṭāpta-karṇa</term>. **Example**: Here, regarding the statement, "divided by the sum of the slow and fast hypotenuses," since that was stated in the context of the **slow-correction procedure** <term>mandaphala-sādhana</term>, then if there is a question as to how it should be done, it is said: the **fast hypotenuse** <term>śīghrakarṇa</term> is to be calculated, and just so, the half-value is to be calculated.

### **Now, the method of observing the conjunction of planets is explained.**

<margin>195</margin> On the "shadow-ground" <note>a plot of land prepared specifically for astronomical observations</note>, the reflection is reversed; one should not look at the tip of one's own shadow. Now, the author explains **Planetary War** <term>yuddha</term> <note>a phenomenon where two planets appear so close that they seem to be competing or "fighting"</note> and **Conjunction** <term>samāgama</term> through two verses:

**Friction** <term>ullekha</term> occurs from the touching of the stars; in **Piercing** <term>bheda</term>, a distinct "splitting" is proclaimed. **Clashing** <term>vimarda</term> is the conflict between them, while **Union** <term>yoga</term> is their mutual meeting. (18)

In a "Superior" war, when [planets] like Mars and the others are endowed with strength and are positioned one below the other in conjunction, a meeting occurs. When the celestial latitude is greater [than the sum of the radii], it is simply a meeting. Regarding the "Touching of the Stars" <note>original: "tārakā-sparśāt"</note>: when the two disks <term>bimba</term> <note>the visible circular face of a planet as seen through an instrument or the naked eye</note> meet at their edges, it is defined as a "Friction War." 

When the latitudes <term>śara</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> are such that the disks appear to overlap or "pierce" one another, the name of that union is "Piercing" <term>bheda</term>. Now, when the rays <term>kiraṇa</term> of both planets touch each other due to the proximity of their latitudes, a "Superior" war occurs. 

In this context, a **Reverse War** <term>apasavya-yuddha</term> <note>literally "left-handed" or "inauspicious" war</note> occurs when one planet is particularly bright or fierce <note>original: "caṇḍa"</note> but has the defect of a small disk area; this is often the case during **retrograde motion** <term>vakra</term> <note>when a planet appears to move backward against the stars</note>.

When the difference in celestial latitude is greater than the sum of the two planetary radii, it is then called a **Meeting** <term>samāgama</term> or **Union** <term>yoga</term>.

When both planets are devoid of brilliance or rays <note>original: "gata-raśmi"; referring to planets that appear dim or are too close to the sun to be seen clearly</note>, it is not considered a **Reverse War** <term>apasavya-yuddha</term> <note>a specific type of inauspicious planetary encounter where the movement appears counter-clockwise</note>. These are to be known as the distinct variations of planetary war. (22)

### The Special Status of Venus
Whether situated in the North or in the South, **Venus** <term>Bhārgava</term> is generally the victor. One should perform the calculation of the conjunction <term>saṃyoga-sādhana</term> based on the various types mentioned previously. (23)

Among the other star-planets <note>original: "itara-grahau"; referring to the other four of the five non-luminary planets: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, if **Venus** <term>Śukra</term> is involved, it is almost always the winner, regardless of whether it is in the northern or southern direction. For these five star-planets starting with **Mars** <term>Bhauma</term>, one should use the established methods of reasoning and calculation to determine the conjunction. (23)

### The Physical Reality of Conjunctions
Now, as to how a "union" <term>saṅgati</term> is possible by the mutual meeting of planets, he says:

**The planets move along their own paths; they are not actually dependent upon or touching one another. Their appearance of "existence" or "non-existence" in union is a matter of perspective.** (24)

These planets travel in "their own paths," meaning their own specific orbits <term>kakṣyā</term>. At the time of a conjunction <term>yuti</term>, they appear to be joined because there is no perceived distance between their centers from our viewpoint on Earth. They "move" or "go" in this state, but because they are at different distances from the observer <note>original: "deśāntareṇa-adarśanāt"; literally "unseen due to the difference in space/distance"</note>, this is why it is called a "Planetary Conjunction." This is the underlying intent. (25)

Regarding the northern <term>somya</term> subjects: in Aries <term>Mesha</term>, the latitude is 7 to the South. <note>original: "dakṣiṇataḥ 7"</note>

The northern stars are said to be thirteen; the southern ones, associated with Rudra and Yama <note>referring to specific deities/regions of the sky</note>, are twenty-seven.

The span <term>bhoga</term> of **Bharani** is 50; since it is multiplied by eight, the result is 400. Due to the singularity of the brought-forward Nakshatra, multiplying by eight yields 800 <note>This likely refers to a specific multiplier used in the Surya Siddhanta for calculating longitudinal positions from the epoch</note>. Thus, for **Krittika**, the resulting position in signs and degrees is 10 [signs], 1 [degree], and 30 [minutes] <note>original: "१० १ ३०"</note>. 

The arc-minutes multiplied by ten should be added to the product of the number twenty-one and its factors. These arc-minutes should then be divided by sixty to derive the value in signs and degrees <note>The text is describing the conversion of total arc-minutes back into the standard units of 30 degrees per sign and 60 minutes per degree</note>. In this manner, the sign-values for all the lunar mansions are fixed.

## Here is an Example ##

Precession <note>original: <term>Ayanāṃśa</term></note>: 18° 38' 57".
The polar longitude of the star <term>Ashwini</term> in signs and degrees: 0 [signs] 78° 0' 0".
The tropical longitude <note>original: <term>Sāyana</term>, the position adjusted for precession</note>: 0 [signs] 25° 35' 57".
The sine of the arc <note>original: <term>Bhujajyā</term></note>: 15 33 23.
The sine of declination <note>original: <term>Krāntijyā</term></note>: 58 26.
The calculated northern declination: 55° 5' 55".
The specific declination degrees for Ashwini: North 5° 55' 15".
The latitude degrees: North 10°.
The sum of these two provides the true declination: North 25° 5' 5' 15".
The distance from the terrestrial latitude toward the south: 15° 36' 1".
The zenith distance <note>original: <term>Natāṃśa</term></note> toward the south: 52° 50' 57".
When these are subtracted from ninety degrees, the altitude degrees <note>original: <term>Unnatāṃśa</term></note> are obtained: 8° 50' 3" 13"'.
This is how the zenith distance and altitude are calculated for all stars.

When a planet is situated at the seventeenth degree of the sign of Taurus, if its southern latitude is extensive, that planet would split the <term>Cart of Rohini</term> <note>the V-shaped cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus, including the bright star Aldebaran; its "splitting" by a planet was traditionally considered a dire omen in Sanskrit astronomy</note>; the meaning is that the planet passes through the very middle of that asterism. 3.

### Calculation of Planetary Conjunctions ###

Now, the method for calculating the <term>Graha-yoga</term> <note>conjunction or alignment of planets with stars</note> is stated. Following the previous rules, one performs the operations using the measurement of the planet's latitude. Just as in the calculations for planetary motion, one uses the planet's daily motion and its latitude. 14.

Just as with the planets, in the absence of latitude, for the purpose of <term>Akṣa-dṛkkarma</term> <note>visibility correction for terrestrial latitude, adjusted for the observer's location</note>, one uses the length of the day and the length of the night. Similarly, for the purpose of the visibility correction, one should apply this to the <term>Dhruvakas</term> <note>fixed polar longitudes</note> of the Sun and the stars based on the lengths of day and night. Here, the correction is mentioned in terms of the <term>Āyana-dṛkkarma</term> <note>visibility correction for the ecliptic, accounting for the tilt of the Earth's axis</note>, as the fixed positions are already established.

Following this, to calculate the remaining conjunctions between stars and planets, one should proceed according to the rules for planetary conjunctions to determine the time elapsed or remaining. The specific detail here is that for the various groups of stars, the result—expressed in days and smaller units—is calculated based solely on the daily motion of the planet. 15.

### Characteristics of Past and Future Conjunctions ###

Now, the rule is given regarding whether the time of a desired conjunction with a star has already passed or is yet to come:

->When the planet's position in a conjunction is greater than the star's fixed longitude, the event is "past." By the reverse logic, the planetary union is known to be "future."<-

Thus ends verse 15. The <term>Āttahṛtkrama</term> <note>original: "आत्तहृत्क्रम"; likely a specific mathematical operation or correction factor</note> is not applied to the corrected <term>Nakṣatradhruva</term> <note>original: "नक्षत्रध्रुव"; the fixed polar longitude of a star</note>.

Regarding the two <term>Vakrāhṛtkrama</term> <note>original: "वक्राहृत्क्रम"; corrections specifically for retrograde motion</note>: when the <term>Sphuṭa-graha</term> <note>original: "स्फुटेग्रहे"; the true or corrected position of the planet</note> is less than the star's longitude, the conjunction—the <term>Nakṣatra-graha-yoga</term> <note>original: "नक्षत्रग्रहयोगः"; the alignment of a planet with a lunar mansion</note>—is "to come" within the desired time interval. If the planet's longitude is greater, the conjunction has already "occurred." However, for a <term>Vakra-graha</term> <note>original: "वक्रग्रहे"; a retrograde planet, which appears to move backward through the zodiac</note>, the opposite is true; because of its reversed motion, the timing of the <term>Samāgama</term> <note>original: "समागमः"; meeting or conjunction</note> in the <term>Nakṣatra-dvayoga</term> <note>original: "नक्षत्रद्वयोगे"; conjunction with the two stars</note> must be understood through this inversion. If the longitude is less, the conjunction is past; if greater, the conjunction is yet to be. 

### 05 Example ###

An <term>Udāharaṇa</term> <note>original: "उदाहरणम्"; a worked mathematical example</note> is now given. For the star <term>Aśvinī</term> <note>original: "अश्विन्त्याः"; the first Nakshatra, associated with the stars in Aries</note>, the established portion is 24° 55' 25". The <term>Akṣajyā</term> <note>original: "षष्ठाक्मज्याया"; the Sine of the terrestrial latitude</note> is 1162' 33". The stated <term>Utkramajyā</term> <note>original: "उक्तमज्या"; the Versine, or versed sine</note> is 10° 3' 8". The <term>Dinavyāsa</term> <note>original: "दिनव्यासः"; the diameter of the day-circle</note> is 33' 35". 

For the star <term>Bharaṇī</term> <note>original: "भरणि"; the second Nakshatra</note>, its <term>Nijyā</term> <note>original: "निज्या"; its specific Sine value</note> is 556' 25". This is multiplied by the <term>Trijyā</term> <note>original: "त्रिजया"; the Radius of the primary circle, usually taken as 3438 minutes</note>, resulting in 2 5 25 2113 <note>these represent large numerical values in sexagesimal or place-value notation</note>. This is then divided by the <term>Dinavyāsadala</term> <note>original: "दिनव्यासदलेन"; half the day-diameter, or the day-radius</note>. 

The resulting <term>Carajyā</term> <note>original: "चरज्या"; the Sine of the ascensional difference, used to determine the variation in rising times</note> is 121' 20". From this, the <term>Ṣaṣṭhīdhanu</term> <note>original: "षष्ठीधनुः"; the arc of the sine in a 60-unit system</note> is produced. All the <term>Carajas</term> <note>original: "चरजाः"; values derived from the ascensional difference</note> are 555' 5" 22"'. 

In this calculation, in place of the usual day-and-night figures, only the <term>Vakrāsarve</term> <note>original: "वक्रासर्वे"; likely the total circular units or specific retrograde arcs</note> are to be taken. This is not done by the previously mentioned method, but by using the <term>Cakrāsarve</term> <note>original: "चक्रासर्वेः"; the total minutes in a circle, 21,600</note> of 21600. The <term>Ṣaṣṭhīdhanu-bhāga</term> <note>original: "षष्ठीधनुः भागः"; the arc portion</note> is 5400, and the second is 5400. 

Because the direction is North, in one place, the <term>Uṣā</term> <note>original: "उषा"; dawn or a specific time arc</note> of 555' 5" 22"' is added to the half-day totals. Elsewhere, it is subtracted, and the <term>Aśvinī-Rādhā</term> <note>original: "अश्विनीराधा"; likely a composite calculation for the stars Ashvini and Vishakha/Radha</note> totals become 5080' 5" 48"'. When these are divided by three hundred and sixty (360), the result is the half-day measured in <term>Ghaṭikās</term> <note>original: "घटिका"; a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>.

<note>original: "athātra budhasyāha"</note>

In the same way, **Mercury** <note>original: "budhaḥ"</note> at twelve and fourteen degrees—when it is **retrograde** <term>vakrī: the apparent backwards motion of a planet in the sky</term> and when its motion is not [fast]—undergoes setting and rising. Mercury, when retrograde and moving with **fast motion** <term>śīghragatiḥ: the phase of an inner planet's orbit when it appears to move most rapidly against the stars</term>, undergoes western setting and eastern rising at twelve degrees of time; for its eastern setting and western rising, Mercury makes its disk [visible/invisible] at fourteen degrees of time.

## **Now he speaks of visibility and invisibility**
<note>original: "atha dṛṣṭādṛṣṭatvamāha"</note>

Planets with greater degrees of time are visible, while those with fewer are invisible in the world; such is the rule for the rising and setting of the two [Venus and Mercury]. For example, as stated before, when they have more than the maximum degrees of time, such as eighteen, they are seen. At the desired time, the planets that are calculated—if they are seen in the calculation for setting, then the "setting" is to be understood; if seen in the calculation for rising, they are "rising." This is the intention. By these fewer degrees of time, the planets become invisible in the world. Being "seen" or "not having reached" [the limit]...

## **Now he speaks of the method for recording the observation**

The form of the disk or orb <note>original: "bimba-svarūpam"</note> is said to be overpowered by the intense rays of the **Sun** <note>original: "sūrya"</note>. Regarding the aforementioned **degrees of time** <term>kālāṃśāḥ: the arc of visibility distance from the Sun</term>: if the desired degrees of time are greater than the limit, the planet is visible; if they are less, it is considered "gone" or invisible. If the degrees are increasing, the planet is rising; if decreasing, it is setting. This is the certain rule.

## **Now, the calculation through daily motion**

The difference in arc minutes <note>original: "antarakalā"</note> should be divided by the difference in **daily motion** <term>bhukti: the distance a planet travels in 24 hours</term>. For **retrograde** <term>vakrī: appearing to move backward</term> planets, one should instead use the sum of the daily motions. 

In this case, 10 is the maximum required degree of time, and the "desired" degree is what we currently have. The difference in arc minutes between these two is divided by the difference in motion between the Sun and the planet. The result provides the time in days and fractions of days. For a retrograde planet, one must divide by the combined motion of the planet and the Sun to find the days remaining until rising or setting.

## **An Example**
<note>original: "udāharaṇam"</note>

Let the desired degree of time be 5° 50' <note>5 degrees and 50 minutes</note> and the maximum required degree be 10°. The difference between them is 4° 10', which equals 250 arc minutes <note>The OCR shows 5 50 as the difference, but the calculation requires the gap between the current position and the visibility limit</note>. 

The difference in motion between the **Sun** and **Venus** <note>original: "śukra"</note> is 15' 32" per day. Dividing the difference by this motion, we obtain 18 days, 45 minutes, and 22 seconds <note>The text uses "dinādi," referring to the division of a day into 60 ghaṭikās</note>. 

This time is applied to the date: **Samvat 1849, the 9th day of the bright fortnight of the month Caitra, Monday** <note>This corresponds to April 1, 1792 CE</note>. By subtracting the result of the calculation from the Sun’s position at sunrise on that Monday, we find the precise longitude of **Venus** for its calculated appearance.

Look now. Regarding the daily motions of the rising sign and the planet: those motions should be calculated to find the time elapsed or remaining, expressed in days and other units. 

The motion of the **Sun** <note>original: "sūrya"</note> and the planet <note>original: "graha"</note> in arc minutes <note>original: "kalā"</note> are adjusted by the rising values of the signs <term>lagnā: the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise on the horizon</term>. These are multiplied by the specific factor and divided by eighteen hundred <note>1800 represents the 1,800 arc minutes in a half-sign of 30 degrees</term>. This provides the "motion in time" <term>kālagati: the daily motion converted into units of time degrees</term> for both the Sun and the planet, allowing one to find the exact days and moments of setting or rising.

## **An Example**
<note>original: "udāharaṇam"</note>

The product, 78341 20, is divided by **eighteen hundred** <note>1800</note>. The result is the Sun’s **motion in time**: 43' 28".

Now for the planet **Venus** <note>original: "śukra"</note>: 
The daily motion of Venus is 75' 24". 
This is multiplied by the same rising value of 13 28. 
The product, 58847 28, is divided by the arc minutes of the sign <note>1800</note>. The result is the motion in time for Venus: 55' 55".

The **desired degrees of time** <note>original: "iṣṭa-kālāṃśa"</note> are 5° 40'. 
The **maximum required degrees of time** <note>original: "parama-kālāṃśa"</note> are 10°. 
The difference between these two is 4° 20', which equals 260 arc minutes. <note>The OCR reads 340, which would correspond to 5° 40'. The text implies the difference between the current visibility and the 10° limit is the focus.</note> 

Using the motion of the Sun (55' 55") and the difference between them, the time remaining is calculated as 10 days, 55 minutes, and 41 seconds <note>original: "dinādi 10 55 41"</note>.

In the year **Samvat 1847**, during the **bright fortnight of the month of Vaishakha** <term>vaiśākha-śukla: the waxing moon phase in April/May</term>, on the 9th lunar day, a Monday, at the time of 7 ghatis, 8 palas, 55 vipalas, and 28 units <note>ghatī: a unit of 24 minutes; pala: 24 seconds</note>, the calculation is adjusted.

After the necessary subtraction, the final result is:
In **Samvat 1847**, during the **dark fortnight of the month of Chaitra** <term>caitra-kṛṣṇa: the waning moon phase in March/April</term>, on the 3rd lunar day, at 7 ghatis, 50 palas, and 45 vipalas from sunrise:
**The Setting of Venus** <note>original: "śukrasyāstaḥ"</note> occurs.

### **The Visibility and Invisibility of the Lunar Mansions**
<note>original: "atha nakṣatra-lokāloka-unāha" — Literally, "Now, he speaks of the looking and non-looking (visibility) of the constellations."</note>

The stars **Svati** <note>Arcturus</note>, **Agastya** <note>Canopus</note>, **Mrigavyadha** <note>Sirius, the 'Deer-Hunter'</note>, **Jyeshtha** <note>Antares</note>, **Punarvasu** <note>Castor and Pollux</note>, **Abhijit** <note>Vega</note>, and **Brahmahridaya** <note>Capella</note>—for each of these, the visibility requirement is **thirteen** degrees. 13 <note>The digit in the manuscript appears as 12, but the text explicitly names "thirteen" (trayodaśa). Now he lists the final group: **Bharani**, **Tishya** <note>Pushya</note>, and **Saumya** <note>Mrigashira</note>... with seven parts... the remaining constellations shine with **seventeen** degrees of visibility. 17.

### **Another Method for Rising and Setting**

Now he states another [rule]:
Rising occurs in the east and setting in the west. When half the circle <note>180 degrees</note> is traversed, the desired day is obtained by dividing by the [motion of the] Sun. || 17 ||

In the west, the rising of the lunar mansions <term>Nakshatras: the 27 or 28 divisions of the sky along the ecliptic</term> is in the east, and their setting is in the west. Behind the lunar mansions, the Sun moves; having left them, it is certain that the attainment of the desired days is calculated by the Sun’s movement, since there is an absence of movement in the fixed stars themselves. || 17 ||

### **Calculation Example**

**Example:**
The arc-minutes for the setting of Venus <term>Shukra: the planet Venus</term> are 10° 42' 4". 
The difference between these two is 5° 50' 55". 
In total minutes: 350' 55". 
Dividing by the difference in daily motion between Venus and the Sun (11' 15"), the result in days and parts of days is 31; 3; 30. 
This same value, when adjusted for the difference of Venus in the observed time <term>drighaṭī: calculated time units based on observation</term>, which is 8; 45; 35, results in the following:
On the 10th day of the bright half of the month of Phalguna <note>roughly February-March</note>, at 9 hours 3 minutes and 55 seconds after sunrise, the setting of Venus occurs.

### **The Stars that Never Set**

Now, regarding the stars that are seen but do not "set" <note>original: "naṣṭodita," referring to stars that remain visible or do not disappear behind the sun's glare</note>:
The stars **Abhijit** <note>Vega</note>, **Shravana**, **Dhanishta** <note>original: "niṣṭhā"</note>, and **Uttara Bhadrapada**, because of their location in the far northern direction, are not reached by the Sun’s rays; that is to say, they are not obscured. They are described as "ever-visible" for this reason. || 18 ||

The resulting **instantaneous Sun** <note>original: *tātkālika sūrya*; the precise position at the moment of the event</note> becomes 2 signs, 5 degrees, 55 minutes, and 27 seconds. 

In the same manner, the **instantaneous Moon** is calculated as 2 signs, 20 degrees, 37 minutes, and 25 seconds. 

The difference between them is 13 degrees, 52 minutes, and 58 seconds. In minutes, this is 832 minutes and 58 seconds.

<meta>This page continues from the discussion on lunar orientations and transitions into the calculation of astronomical nodes or conjunctions known as Patas. Specifically, it defines the conditions for the Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta alignments, which occur when the Sun and Moon reach specific positions relative to each other and the celestial equator.</meta>

<meta>Digital watermark at bottom: CC-0 Dharmartha Trust J&K. An eGangotri-Vaidika Bharata Initiative</meta>

Those called the equal **Vaidhṛta** <term>vaidhṛti</term> [alignments] are as follows: 1. If the Sun and the Moon, adjusted for precession <term>sāyana</term> <note>original: 'sāyanau', meaning the coordinates include the precession of the equinoxes</note>, are situated in the same solstice or hemisphere <term>ayana</term>—meaning they are both in either the Northern or the Southern hemisphere—at that time, when their longitudinal positions are added together and the sum equals twelve signs <note>original: 'māṇḍale dvādaśa rāśiṣu', representing a full 360-degree circle</note>, and if the declinations <term>krānti</term> of the Sun and Moon are equal, then that great alignment <term>pāta</term> is known as **Vaidhṛti** <term>vaidhṛti</term>. 

Now he explains the possibility of the alignment known as **Vyatīpāta** <term>vyatīpāta</term>. When the Sun and Moon are in opposite hemispheres <term>ayana</term>, and their declinations are equal, then **Vyatīpāta** occurs when the sum of their positions equals half a circle <note>original: 'bhagaṇārdhena', literally half a revolution or 180 degrees</note>. 2. If the Sun and the Moon, with precessional adjustment, are in different hemispheres, and the sum of the positions of the Sun and Moon equals six signs, and their minutes of declination <term>krānti-kalā</term> are equal, then at that moment, the alignment named **Vyatīpāta** occurs. 2.

The **Tropical Moon** <term>sāyana-candra</term> is 10 [signs], 23 [degrees], 15 [minutes], 11 [seconds].

Now, the sum of these two is 0 [signs], 20 [degrees], 58 [minutes], 5 [seconds]. Subtracting this from twelve signs <note>representing a full circle of 360 degrees</note>, the remainder is 10 [signs], 58 [minutes], 5 [seconds].
The excess... the node has passed; these are the digits: 85, 8, 5.
Dividing by the combined motion of the Sun and Moon (810; 58), the resulting time in days is 0; 58, 17, 17. By applying this motion to the desired time, the **instantaneous Sun** is 11 [signs], 9 [degrees], 15 [minutes], 8 [seconds]. The **Moon** is 10 [signs], 11 [degrees], 55 [minutes], 56 [seconds]. Their sum is 0 [signs], 0 [degrees], 0 [minutes], 0 [seconds].

The **node** <term>pāta</term> is 2 [signs], 13 [degrees], 30 [minutes].
For the **Tropical Sun** at 11 [signs], 25 [degrees], 5 [minutes], 17 [seconds], the **sine** <term>jyā</term> is 2035; 58. Multiplied by the **sine of maximum declination** <term>parama-krāntijyā</term> <note>the sine of the obliquity of the ecliptic, traditionally 1397 in this system</note> of 1397, the product is 343151; 14, 118.
Dividing by the **standard radius** <term>trijyā</term> <note>the radius of the calculation circle, usually 3438 minutes</note> of 3438, the obtained **sine of declination** <term>krāntijyā</term> is 1058; 59. From the arc of this sine, the Sun's declination in minutes is determined as 1035; 58.

The **Tropical Moon** is 10 [signs], 11 [degrees], 55 [minutes], 53 [seconds]. The **arm** <term>bhuja</term> <note>the angular distance from the nearest equinoctial point</note> is 1 [sign], 15 [degrees], 15 [minutes], 17 [seconds]. Its **sine** <term>jyā</term> is 2990; 58.
Multiplied by the sine of maximum declination (1397), the result is 1841159; 54, 16.
Divided by the radius, the obtained **sine of declination** is 1058; 59.

### The General Method of the Three Verses

Now, [the author] explains the general method for the twenty-eight [astronomical divisions] <note>likely referring to the mahāpātas or the divisions of the ecliptic</note> in three verses:

The sine of the declination <term>krāntijyā</term> is divided, and the distance in **yojanas** <note>a unit of distance, here used in an astronomical context for angular measurement</note> between the declinations is found. Whether the node is **yet to occur** <term>bhāvi</term> or has **already passed** <term>gata</term> depends on the movement. (10)

The difference in the centers [of the Sun and Moon] is calculated by the motion. When the Sun is multiplied by the sine of the arm <term>bhujajyā</term>, the result is in **minutes of arc** <term>liptā</term> and so on. The result of the calculation for the node of the Moon should be applied in the **reverse order** <note>original: "viparyayāt"; implying a subtraction instead of an addition, or vice versa</note>. This process should be **repeated several times** <note>original: "asakṛd-āvartaved"; referring to the iterative method used in Indian astronomy to reach precision</note> until the times are equal. (11)

### Commentary and Practical Calculation

The declinations of the **Sun and Moon** <note>original: "sūryacandrayoḥ"</note> should be calculated. When the **radius** <term>trijyā</term> <note>the standard radius used in sine tables, usually 3438 minutes</note> is multiplied and divided by the **maximum sine of declination** <term>parama-krāntijyā</term>, the resulting arcs <term>dhanuṣī</term> <note>literally "bows"</note> of those two should be determined. 

The difference between these two arcs, in **minutes** <term>liptā</term> and so on, represents the time of the node—whether it is **yet to occur** <note>original: "bhāvi"</note> or has **passed**. If the distance is to be traversed by the Moon, the calculation should be made according to the Moon's daily motion. 

When the node is near, the **Vajra** <note>original: "vajraḥ"; likely a technical term for a specific alignment or a corrective factor in the Pāta calculation</note> occurs. In that case, at the end of the quadrant, the difference is multiplied by the **sine of the sum** <term>yogajyā</term> and divided by its own **daily motion** <term>gatyā</term>. The result, in minutes and seconds, is applied to the Sun and Moon. 

Just as the calculation is performed when the degrees are lacking, the same is done for the Sun. The result for the **lunar node** <term>candra-pāta</term> <note>the ascending or descending node, Rahu or Ketu</note> is determined by the distance and the motion. Divided by its own specific motion, the result obtained should be applied in the **opposite direction** <note>original: "viparyayāt"</note>; thus the true position of the lunar node is established.

The aforementioned process should be performed **repeatedly** <note>original: "asakṛd"; referring to an iterative mathematical method used to reach higher precision</note> until the **true declinations** <term>spaṣṭa-krānti</term> <note>the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the Sun and Moon are brought into agreement through the method of successive approximation. This is the procedure. (1)

### Practical Example

**Solar Declination** <term>sūrya-krānti</term>: 10° 35' 58"
The **sine of the latitude** <term>akṣajīvā</term> is 0° 58' 8". This is multiplied by the **radius** <term>trijyā</term> <note>the standard radius of 3438' 52" 28 used in trigonometric calculations</note>. When divided by the **sine of the maximum declination** <term>parama-krāntijyā</term> <note>the sine of the Earth's axial tilt, approximately 24 degrees in this system</note> of 1397, the result obtained is 25|05|13. The corresponding **arc** <term>cāpa</term> for this value is 24° 54' 58".

**Lunar Declination** <term>candra-krānti</term>: 13° 55' 21"
Its **sine** <term>jyā</term> is 1358|55. When multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of maximum declination, the result is 3225|55. The corresponding **arc** <term>cāpa</term> is 42° 28' 53".

The difference between these two arcs in **minutes of arc** <term>kalāntara</term> is 1233' 59". 

Because the position of the **node** <term>pāta</term> must be made precise: 
For the **tropical Moon** <term>sāyana-candra</term> <note>the Moon's position adjusted for the precession of the equinoxes</note> at 10 signs 10° 55' 53", the newly calculated Moon is 9 signs 11° 18' 52".

Taking those same minutes of difference (1233' 59") and multiplying by the **daily motion of the Sun** <term>ravi-gati</term> (59' 34"), the result is 73091|50. This is then divided by the **daily motion of the Moon** <term>candra-gati</term> (750' 22"). The resulting **correction in minutes** <term>kalādi-phala</term> is 97' 42". The correction for the Sun and other factors is 1° 35' 52".

From the previously stated tropical Sun at 1 sign 24° 25' 3", the **corrected Sun** <term>punar-jātaḥ sūryaḥ</term> becomes 1 sign 20° 45' 49".

Using that same difference in arcs (1233' 59") multiplied by the **motion of the node** <term>pāta-gati</term> (3' 11"), we get 3822|8. Divided by the Moon's daily motion (750' 22"), the result in minutes is 5' 15". 

Since the node moves in **reverse** <note>original: "viparītatvāt"; referring to the retrograde motion of the lunar nodes</note>, this value is **subtracted** from the node's position of 0 signs 22° 37' 39". The resulting corrected node is 0 signs 22° 12' [39"].

### Determining if the Node has Passed or is Approaching

Now, the author describes whether the **time of the Node** <term>pāta-kāla</term> has passed or is yet to come relative to **midnight** <term>ardharātra</term>:

->**When the declinations are equal, it is the Node. If the Moon is less [than the required position] at midnight, the Node has passed; if the Moon is greater at that time, the Node is yet to occur.** 11<-

Thus, by iterative calculation, when the **true declinations** <term>spaṣṭa-krānti</term> of the Sun and Moon are equal, the **Node** <term>pāta</term> occurs. <note>This "Node" refers to *Mahapata*, a specific astronomical aspect where the Sun and Moon reach the same declination, considered highly significant in Vedic astronomy for timing rituals.</note>

It concludes with a rule for determining if this celestial alignment occurred before or after midnight based on the Moon's longitudinal position.</summary>
<keywords>declination, Kranti-samya, Sun, Moon, Pata, sine, mathematical astronomy, midnight calculation, iterative process</keywords>

--- Page 1147 ---
<meta>This page continues the iterative refinement process described on the previous page. Having calculated the declinations, the text now moves to determining the precise moment of "declination equality" (krānti-sāmya) relative to midnight and sunrise.</meta>

The **middle time** <term>madhya-kāla</term> would be the time of **midnight** <term>ardha-rātri-kālika</term> derived from the **observation** <term>vedha</term> of the **equality of declinations of the Moon and Sun** <term>candrārka-krānti-sāmya</term>. This is calculated from the **difference of the arcs of declination** <term>krānti-cāpāntara</term> and by the half-sum brought from that calculation. The observation is thus established. If this value is less than the midnight value, the **middle time of the node’s occurrence** <term>pāta-sampāta-madhya-kāla</term> is said to have already passed. If the observation at the time of declination equality is greater than the observation at midnight, it means the **time of the node** <term>pāta-kāla</term> is yet to occur after the time of midnight.

### Explaining the Knowledge of the Time of the True Node
<term>spaṣṭa-pāta-kāla-jñāna</term>

The difference between the Sun and Moon at the **stabilized midnight** <term>sthirī-kṛta-ardharātra</term> should be multiplied by sixty and divided by the [difference in] **motions** <term>bhrama</term>; the result is the **minutes of time** <term>nāḍikā</term> of the time of the Node. || 13 ||

<note>This verse provides a standard mathematical formula (rule of three) to convert the angular distance between the celestial bodies into the time remaining until they reach the point of equal declination.</note>

The "stabilized midnight Sun and Moon" refers to the positions of the Sun and Moon at midnight, calculated through the **iterative process** <term>asakṛt-karma</term>. The **observation** <term>vedha</term> is the midnight observation. The **difference in minutes** <term>antara-kalā</term> between those two is **multiplied by sixty** <term>ṣaṣṭyā guṇitāḥ</term> and **divided** <term>bhaktāḥ</term> by the **speed of the true observation** <term>spaṣṭa-vedha-gati</term>. The resulting **time units** <term>ghaṭikā</term> represent the time of the true declination equality. If these occur before midnight, they are subtracted from the elapsed time; if after, they are added. This gives the **middle time of the node** <term>pāta-madhya-kāla</term> in elapsed time units starting from **sunrise** <term>sūryodaya</term>.

Now, one might ask: for how long does the state of the Node last? The text says:
As long as the difference [between declinations] is less than the **sum of the diameters** <term>māna-yoga</term> [of the Sun and Moon], for that long the state of **declination equality** <term>krānti-sāmya</term> exists. || 1 ||

<note>This explains that the astronomical "node" is not a single point in time but a duration, lasting as long as the two celestial disks overlap in terms of their declination.</note>

This result, in units such as **time units** <term>ghaṭikā</term>, should always be applied to the **combined time** <term>miśra-kāla</term>. Then, from the sixty [ghaṭikās of a day], one finds the middle of the node from sunrise on that day.

It defines the formula to convert angular distance into time and explains that the event has a duration based on the combined sizes of the solar and lunar disks.</summary>

### Calculation Example
<term>udāharaṇam</term>

The **stabilized Moon** <term>sthirīkṛta-candra</term> <note>The Moon's position after applying iterative corrections for accuracy.</note> is at 10 [signs], 0 [degrees], 12 [minutes], 42 [seconds].
The **midnight Moon** <term>ardha-rātrika-candra</term> is at 10 [signs], 5 [degrees], 54 [minutes], 39 [seconds].

In this instance, following the stated method, because the calculated value is greater than the midnight value, the time [of the node] is yet to occur. The difference between the two [Moon positions] is 103 [degrees], 1 [minute], 8 [seconds], 52 [thirds]. The remaining **minutes** <term>kalās</term> are 18 and 52 [seconds]. Multiplying this by **sixty** <term>ṣaṣṭyā</term> gives 1122. These are the **time-units** <term>ghaṭikās</term> of the node within a sixty-unit cycle: 1 [and] 10.

### Calculating the Half-Duration of the Node
<term>pāta-kāla-śasinyardhānayana</term>

Now, the author explains the method for finding the half-duration of the node:
One should multiply **half the sum of the diameters of the Sun and Moon** <term>ravīndu-māna-yogārdhaṃ</term> by sixty, and divide that by the **difference in their daily motions** <term>bhukty-antarā</term>. The **result** <term>labdhi</term> provides the **half-duration** <term>sty-ardha</term> in **time-units** <term>nāḍikā</term> and so on. || 15 ||

As described in the section on **Lunar Eclipses** <term>candra-grahaṇa</term>, one should take the sum of the radii <note>Literally "half the diameters"</note> of the **Sun and Moon** <term>sūrya-candra</term> in minutes. Multiply that half-sum by sixty and divide by the **difference in the true motions** <term>spaṣṭa-gaty-antara</term> of the Sun and Moon, expressed in minutes.

The result obtained is the half-duration. When this is applied to the **time of the node** <term>pāta-kāla</term>, the period of the node's occurrence is established, spanning from the beginning until the end of that time.

### The Beginning and Middle Times of the Node
<term>pāta-madhyādi-kāla</term>

The author now states:
The **middle time** <term>madhya-kāla</term> of the node, when decreased or increased by the **half-duration** <term>ardha-sthityā</term>, gives the times of its **possible occurrence** <term>sambhava-kāla</term>. These are designated as the "beginning" and "end" [of the node]. || 16 ||

The **true time of the node** <term>spaṣṭa-pāta-kāla</term> brought forth by the previously mentioned method is considered the middle...

<page-num>170</page-num>

<margin>On Monday, the 3rd.</margin>
From the sum of the astronomical times, 5:10 is the resulting **meritorious time** <term>puṇyakāla</term> <note>A sacred window of time for performing rituals, usually during an eclipse or conjunction.</note>. This should be understood as appropriate for determining the **evening hour** <term>pradoṣa-velā</term>.

The "scissors-like" <note>original: "kartarī"</note> movement is traditionally understood through the term "continuous motion." Therefore, the division must be performed by the **difference in motion** <term>gatyantara</term> of the Sun and Moon. This is the meaning: to calculate the **half-duration of the contact** <term>sparśa-sthityardha</term> <note>The time from the start of the conjunction to its midpoint.</note>, for a single day, one must divide the **sum of the radii** <term>māna-yoga-dala</term> multiplied by sixty by the **difference in motion** <term>gatyantara</term> <gloss>motion</gloss> of the Sun and Moon.

To calculate the **half-duration of the release** <term>mokṣa-sthityardha</term> <note>The time from the midpoint of the conjunction to its end.</note>, for a single day, the wise should divide the **sum of the radii** <term>māna-yoga-dala</term> multiplied by sixty by the **difference in motion** <term>gatyantara</term> of the Sun and Moon. This calculation must be performed repeatedly <note>An iterative process where the result of one calculation is used to refine the next.</note> until the **difference in motion** <term>gatyantara</term> becomes equal to the **sum of the radii** <term>māna-yoga-dala</term>. This is the summary.

Here is another special rule: In the event of a **Vaidhṛta** <term>vaidhṛta</term> <note>A specific astronomical alignment where the Sun and Moon are in opposite hemispheres but have equal declination.</note>, the difference of the two motions is the divisor when the directions are different, and the sum is the divisor when the directions are the same. In the event of a **Vyatīpāta** <term>vyatīpāta</term> <note>An alignment where the Sun and Moon are in the same hemisphere with equal declination.</note>, the difference of the motions is the divisor when the directions are the same, and the sum is the divisor when the directions are different.

### **Example**
<term>udāharaṇe</term>

The **tropical Sun** <term>sāyana-ravi</term> <note>The Sun's position measured from the vernal equinox.</note> is established as: 11 [signs], 28 [degrees], 25 [minutes], 35 [seconds]. For the calculation of the **duration of the release** <term>mokṣa-sthityardha</term>, the **true motion** <term>spaṣṭa-gati</term> of 59' 25" is subtracted. The result for the previous day is 11 [signs], 27 [degrees], 25 [minutes], 55 [seconds].

The **tropical Moon** <term>sāyana-candra</term> is established as: 10 [signs], 25 [degrees], 10 [minutes], 41 [seconds]. Subtracting the **true motion** <term>spaṣṭa-gati</term> of 792' 24", the result for the previous day's Moon is 10 [signs], 12 [degrees], 35 [minutes], 35 [seconds].

The **node** <term>pāta</term> is established as: 9 [signs], 22 [degrees], 22 [minutes], 25 [seconds]. Adding the motion of 3' 11", the result for the previous day's node is 9 [signs], 22 [degrees], 30 [minutes], 22 [seconds].

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of astronomical conjunctions (Pātas), specifically moving from the general concept of equal declination to the specific calculation of the Vyatīpāta Yoga—the 17th among the twenty-seven astrological yogas—and providing a mathematical example for its determination.</meta>

...through the reversal of the arc, its absence occurs when the **declinations** <term>krānti</term> <note>Declination is the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the two—the Sun and the Moon—are not unequal. This means they are equal. The declination of the Sun is the "corrected" declination; when these two are known to be equal, [the conjunction occurs]. 1 ॥

### The Determination of the Vyatīpāta Conjunction

Now, the knowledge of the **Vyatīpāta** <term>vyatīpāta</term> <note>original: "vyatīpāta"; literally "falling away" or "transgression," referring to a specific inauspicious astrological period.</note> conjunction is explained. The sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon, as previously mentioned, is converted into minutes of arc <term>liptā</term> and divided by the **arc of a constellation** <term>bhabhoga</term> <note>original: "bhabhoga"; the space occupied by one lunar mansion, defined as 800 minutes of arc.</note>. If the resulting value falls at the end of the seventeenth [yoga], it is known as the "Third Vyatīpāta." 10

Furthermore, for the Sun and Moon—when their positions in signs and degrees are converted into **minutes of arc** <term>kalā</term> and divided by the *bhabhoga* of a nakshatra, which is **eight hundred** <note>800 minutes.</note>—the result is the seventeenth. From the end of the sixteenth until the seventeenth is reached, that is the other Vyatīpāta, the third one. In the counting of the yogas starting from **Viṣkambha** <note>The first of the 27 astrological yogas.</note>, Vyatīpāta should be recognized as the seventeenth.

Now, regarding its effects: It is **inauspicious** <term>aśubha-kara</term> for all celebratory or auspicious rites, but it is **merit-bestowing** <term>śubha-da</term> for acts such as **charity** <term>dāna</term> and similar religious offerings. 10 ॥

### Mathematical Example

**The Sun and Moon:**
The Sun: 5 Signs, 3°, 2', 55"
The Moon: 10 Signs, 1°, 23', 1"
**Their Sum:** 15 Signs, 10°, 5', 58"

The minutes of arc for this sum are 10,555 and 58 seconds <note>Calculation: (15 signs * 30 deg * 60 min) + (10 deg * 60 min) + 5 min = 27000 + 600 + 5 = 27605. The OCR "1055" likely refers to a specific step in the division or a manuscript shorthand.</note>. This is divided by **eight hundred** (800). By the counting starting with Viṣkambha, one should find the yoga. In that calculation, the seventeenth yoga is Vyatīpāta; it should be known by this name.

Now, the knowledge arising from the **junction points** <term>gaṇḍānta</term> <note>Original: "gaṇḍānta"; refers to the inauspicious "knot-ends" or junctions between certain zodiac signs and lunar mansions.</note> and the constellation arcs is stated:

For the junctions of **Revatī**, **Ashvinī**, and others, the transition between them is considered. The final part of the previous [constellation] and the initial part of the following one is famously called **Gandānta** <term>gandānta</term> <note>original: "gaṇḍānta"; literally the "end of the cheek" or "knot-end," referring to the spiritually volatile junctions between water and fire signs in the zodiac.</note>. ॥

At the end of the constellations of **Ashleṣā**, **Jyeṣṭhā**, and **Revatī**, and the beginning of those that follow—namely **Maghā**, **Mūla**, and **Ashvinī**—the transition occurs. This is known as the **midpoint of the junction** <term>nakṣatra-madhya</term>. For these, specifically Ashleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī, the latter half of the constellation is combined with the first quarter of the following constellation to determine what is observed as **Gandānta**. By this very definition, even minor activities are forbidden during these times. 21 

### On the Prohibition of Activities

Now, the prohibition of other activities is stated. ॥ During the **Vyatīpāta** <note>A specific inauspicious astronomical conjunction.</note> yoga and the three types of **Gandānta**, one should avoid all rituals. To ward off the faults arising from these periods, one should refrain from all initiated works. 22 

The conclusion of **Vyatīpāta**, as well as the transition points of Revatī and Ashvinī, are to be treated as Vyatīpāta itself. In the same way, one must consider the three **Gandāntas** <note>The three junctions are: 1. Ashlesha/Magha, 2. Jyeshtha/Mula, 3. Revati/Ashvini.</note> at the end of those constellations. All of these points should be avoided in secret practices or specialized rituals. 22 ॥ 

### The Master Concludes the Teaching

Now, the person who has explained these matters concludes with the words of the sage **Vasiṣṭha** <note>A famous Vedic seer (Rishi) to whom many astronomical and legal texts are attributed.</note>: ॥

**"Thus, this supreme secret regarding the movement of the stars and dates has been told for your benefit. O great-minded one, this has been declared by me; what else do you wish to hear?"** 
२३ ॥ 

**Hemādri** <note>Likely referring to the author or the famous 13th-century polymath whose "Chaturvarga Chintamani" is a standard reference for such rituals.</note> says: I have declared this secret, which is the progenitor of all six [limbs of Vedānga], and which is extremely hidden and most necessary for action. Beyond this, what other secret regarding these matters do you wish to hear? ॥ 

By this, the entire body of the **Vedas** <term>veda-traya-deha</term> <note>original: "vedatrayadeha"; the "body of the three Vedas."</note> is honored; in every instance, one should perform duties with a steady and focused mind.

The **Chapter on the Sphere** <term>golādhyāya</term> <note>The section of Indian astronomical texts dedicated to spherical geometry, planetary models, and cosmology.</note> is now being explained. ॥ 1 ॥ Having been instructed by the Guru, **Mayasura** <note>In the Sūrya Siddhānta, Maya is a demon (asura) who receives divine astronomical knowledge from a representative of the Sun God.</note> asked the Sage with a composed mind. Then, looking up toward the heavens, he offered a respectful salutation with folded hands and inquired about the revolutions of the celestial bodies, the mathematical cycles, and the shadows. ॥ 1 ॥

After hearing the words previously spoken, the demon **Maya** asked again for specific details. Standing with joined palms, he inquired about the celestial revolutions currently in motion. He asked: "O Blessed Lord, what is the **measure** <term>pramāṇa</term> of the Earth? What is its **shape** <term>ākāra</term>? Upon what does it **rest** <term>āśraya</term>? What are its **divisions**? And how do the heavens revolve around the underworld?" ॥ 2 ॥

"O Blessed Lord, what is the size of the Earth previously mentioned? Is there a definitive measurement for it or not?" This is the intent of the question. He asks for the calculation used in astronomy to describe the planetary revolutions. "What is its shape? Between a flat, forest-like expanse and a spherical form, which is the actual shape of the Earth?" This is the question regarding its form. "Upon what does it rest?" <note>Maya's questions reflect the shift from observational rules to the underlying physical and mathematical model of a spherical Earth suspended in space.</note>

**"O Lord <term>Bhagavan</term>, Creator of all Beings <term>Bhūta-bhāvana</term>, cut through this doubt of mine. Besides You, there is no one else capable of destroying this uncertainty for us." ॥ 9 ॥**

**"O Blessed Lord, Creator of all Beings"** means the one who is the source of the existence and manifestation of all living things. 

The meaning is: "Cut through this [doubt] of mine which has arisen—cut through these questions. Other than You, no one else is found or exists as a 'destroyer of doubt' <term>saṃśaya-cchettā</term>." ॥ 9 ॥

**Now, regarding the questions spoken by Maya:**

The Supreme Person spoke to the Sage; he speaks back to the Sage. **"Thus, having heard what the devotee said,"** I have not [merely] composed a sentence, but having resolved this secret <term>rahasya</term>, the Lord speaks again to the virtuous ones. ॥ 10 ॥ There, the Supreme Person goes toward that Maya [to answer] the resolution of his questions. That which is indeed a secret for men, the Lord of All <term>Sarveśvara</term> spoke to you. He acts as a bridge to the previous [knowledge]. 

By this, he has spoken. In [the phrase] "to the endless one," the speech requires the previously mentioned knowledge. In the manner described, with devotion <term>bhaktyā</term>, the questions that were spoken and raised have been heard by me. ॥ 10 ॥ 

In that regard, demonstrating a feeling of grace, the Supreme Person said to Maya:

**"Fix your mind <term>manas</term> on Me alone; let your intellect <term>buddhi</term> dwell within Me."**

<vocab>bhagavan: Lord or Blessed One; saṃśaya: doubt; praśna: question; muni: sage; bhūta-bhāvana: the creator or sustainer of all beings; rahasya: secret or esoteric knowledge; bhakti: devotion; manas: the sensory or thinking mind; buddhi: the higher intellect or faculty of discernment.</vocab>

<summary>Mayasura concludes his technical questions by asking the Sun God to clear his doubts, acknowledging Him as the only true source of cosmic knowledge. The Sun God begins his revelation by instructing Maya to focus his mind and intellect entirely on the divine source to receive the "secret" knowledge of the stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the deity Aniruddha's manifestation. Following the description of the "Golden Womb" (Hiranyagarbha) on page 177, this section details how Aniruddha takes the form of the Sun (Surya) to organize time and the physical universe through the power of the three Vedas.</meta>

<page-num>178</page-num>

His nature is the Lotus, and he is known by the name **Aniruddha**; thus is he defined and explained in the Vedas, the Puranas, and other sacred scriptures. This is the very nature of the Sun (**Surya**): the hymns of the **Rigveda** constitute his solar orb; the hymns of the **Samaveda** are his rays <note>original: "ustrāḥ"</note>; and the hymns of the **Yajurveda** are his physical form <term>mūrti</term>. Thus, the Lord is composed of the three-fold Veda <term>trayīmaya</term>. 

This Lord is the **Soul of Time** <term>Kālātma</term>, the very embodiment of time, and the Maker of Time. Through the cycles of creation, preservation, and dissolution, he is the all-powerful and capable Lord. He is the **Soul of All** <term>Sarvātma</term>, whose nature is the universe itself. He is all-pervading, present everywhere, and remains eternal. It is said that the entire world is established within the Sun. ॥ 18 ॥

He consists of the wheel of moments <term>nimiṣa</term> and the various divisions of time <term>kalā</term>. Being of the nature of the year <term>saṃvatsara</term>, and joined with the progression of days and nights, he perpetually orbits the universe. ॥ 18 ॥ 

As the soul of the three worlds, he is the wheel composed of years and months. Comprising the divisions of the year and joined with day and night, he orbits eternally. Because of this, the Sun revolves there constantly and without interruption; the days and nights are joined into months, beginning with the sign of the Ram <note>original: "meṣāditaḥ," referring to Aries and the start of the solar zodiacal year</note>. ॥ 19 ॥

Three-quarters of his brilliance remained unmanifest, while one-quarter became the foundation of this world. The Lord, the "I Am" <note>original: "soham"</note> and the ultimate Cause, created **Brahma** to act as the creator of the manifest world. ॥ 20 ॥ 

Of this Soul of the Vedas, three of his divine steps <note>original: "tripāta-caraṇātraye"</note> remain in the celestial realm, grasped only by the mind. His fourth quarter, however, became visible to all in this world. Thus is described the Lord known by the name **Aniruddha**.

<summary>This page describes the Sun (Surya) as a manifestation of Aniruddha, explaining how the three Vedas form the Sun's body and how he governs the cycles of time and the zodiac. It also touches upon the "Purusha" concept where only one-quarter of the divine is manifest in the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>Aniruddha, Surya, Sun, Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Time (Kala), Zodiac (Meshadi), Brahma, Creation, Trayimaya</keywords>

Being fully capable as the instrumental cause for the creation of the universe, from the **Cosmic Ego** <term>Ahaṃkāra</term>, and through that very form of Ego, He produced **Brahma** the Cosmic Person <term>Puruṣa</term> within the world. ॥ 20 ॥ To him, the **Grandfather of All Worlds** <note>original: "sarvaloka-pitāmahaḥ," a common epithet for Brahma as the first progenitor</note>, He granted the **Vedas**. <meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical creation of the Sun and Moon described on the previous page to mathematical geography and astronomy. It discusses the relationship between the Sun's position at the equinox, the shadow cast in equatorial regions, and the geometry of the Earth relative to the celestial poles (Mount Meru).</meta>

When the **Sun** <term>Divākara; literally "The Day-Maker"</term> is situated at the **Equinox** <term>Viṣuva</term>, the degrees of the **Zenith distance** <term>Natāṃśa; the angular distance from the point directly overhead</term> constitute the equinoctial shadow. In this specific orientation, it is said that no [other] shadow exists. ॥ 42 ॥ 

When the Sun is positioned at the Equinox, it passes directly over the **equatorial cities** <note>original: "nagarīṇām," referring to cities on the terrestrial equator</note>. It revolves through the meridian of those cities; at that time, the "Equinoctial Shadow" is defined as the midday shadow. In the presence of the Sun, the elevation of the center is determined by the degrees of the zenith distance. Therefore, [through technical calculation] the state of solar elevation is established. ॥ 42 ॥

**Mount Meru** <note>In Indian cosmology, Meru represents the North Pole or the central axis of the world</note> exists at both [poles]. In the descent from the center, the position of the heavens for the **Equatorial regions** <term>Nirakṣa; literally "without latitude"</term> arises for both horizons. ॥ 43 ॥ 

Like a staff <term>Daṇḍakam</term>, the axis extends from Meru toward both the South and the North; this is observed as a straight line in the sky. These two points are to be understood as the **Poles** <term>Dhruva; the "Fixed" or "Immovable" points</term>. For the people living in the **Equatorial regions**, the **Horizon** <term>Kṣitija; literally "Earth-born"</term> is clearly formed where the earth and the sky-waters meet. ॥ 43 ॥

Therefore, because of the zenith distance of those two Poles situated on the horizon, an angle of ninety degrees is formed at Mount Meru. ॥ 44 ॥ 

For this reason, in those [equatorial] cities, because the Sun is not displaced from the Pole [in terms of relative latitude] and the two Poles sit upon the horizon, a full ninety degrees is obtained. In the Equatorial region, because there is an absence of latitude at Meru <note>meaning the observer at the equator sees the pole at a zero-degree elevation, but the distance to the zenith is 90 degrees</note>, the count of the maximum zenith distance is established. ॥ 45 ॥

<summary>This text explains the geometry of the Earth and sky, focusing on how the Sun's position at the equinox creates specific shadows at the equator and how the North and South Poles (Meru) define the global axis.</summary>
<keywords>Equinox, Mount Meru, Zenith distance, Equatorial regions, Celestial Poles, Sun, Shadow calculation, Jyotisha</keywords>

This means that for those dwelling by the sea, this "girdle" stands as a fixed boundary for the purpose of separating the divine and demonic territories. From this girdle, one side is the **land of the gods** <term>Deva-bhūmi</term>, and to the south lies the land belonging to the others. ॥ 37 ॥

All around the central portion of Meru, it is understood that there are **islands** <term>Dvīpa</term> provided for the sake of the gods. ॥ 38 ॥

From the middle of Meru—the central point of the axis—extending outward rapidly through the regions of space, from the highest station of Meru reaching up to the heavens, the sky is filled with heat. In those islands, the land is established for the sake of the gods. ॥ 39 ॥

In the seventh region is the famous city known as **Yamakoti** <term>Yamakāṭī; traditionally one of the four cardinal cities on the equator, specifically the one to the East</term>. This is a great city with golden gateways and fortifications. To the south, in the region of **Bharata** <term>Bhārata-varṣa</term>, stands a magnificent great city. ॥ 9 <note>The numeral here likely refers to a sub-section or a local numbering system</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the relative nature of direction and the Earth’s shape. Following the previous page’s argument that "up" and "down" are subjective, this section explains why the Earth, though spherical, appears flat to its inhabitants, and how the celestial rotation is perceived differently by the Gods and the Demons.</meta>

Here, it is established that there is no absolute "below." For those in the lower regions, <note>Referring to inhabitants of the opposite side of the globe</note> the Earth is situated in the center of the **Universe** <term>Brahmanda; literally 'the Egg of Brahma,' representing the cosmos</term>. Because of its **spherical shape** <term>vartalakarata</term>, it is situated equally in space on all sides. 

Since the Earth is a sphere, the concept of "up" and "down" is entirely relative to one’s position. By calculating the "upward" and "downward" states <note>original: "urdhva-adhara-bhava"</note> relative to where one stands, one understands how everything is held. ॥ 52 ॥

Here, an objection is raised: If the Earth is a **sphere** <term>golakara</term>, why is this not directly perceived by our eyes? Why does it appear as a flat surface, like a mirror? To this, he says: 

Because of the **smallness of the scale** <term>alpakarata</term> of the people on the Earth, they cannot see the entire surface from any single position. Just as one sees only a tiny portion of a massive curve, it appears as a flat level rather than a **curved shape** <term>vakra-kara</term>. ॥ 55 ॥

The explanation follows: People, due to the tiny size of their bodies relative to the vastness of the Earth, perceive only the immediate vicinity of their location. No matter which direction they look, they cannot grasp the **spherical curvature** <term>vartala-manika</term>. They see only a minute portion, which appears straight. Even though the Earth is a sphere, the measurement of the visible area is so small that the mind perceives it as a flat plane. ॥ 55 ॥

Furthermore, the celestial sphere rotates for the **Gods** <term>Devas; located at the North Pole</term> and for the **Demons** <term>Asuras; located at the South Pole</term>. Above them, those who are situated there see the stars always moving toward the **West** <term>pashchimamukha; west-facing</term>. ॥ 55 ॥ 

Just as a person at the North Pole sees the stars moving in one direction, so too do those at the South Pole, but relative to their own position. For the Gods, the rotation proceeds in one order, while for the Demons, it proceeds in another. This makes it clear that the perception of motion depends on the observer's location on the globe. ॥ 55 ॥

<summary>This page explains that the Earth is a sphere suspended in the center of the universe, and it addresses the common perception of a flat Earth as an illusion caused by the observer's small size. It also describes how the stars appear to move westward for observers at both poles.</summary>

Who is there who does not know the **day of the equinox** <term>Vishuvat; the day when day and night are of equal length</term> occurring near the end of the season?

From this point forward, regarding the **Celestial Sphere** <term>Gola</term>:

This is the meaning: 
In the **Region of the Gods** <note>the North</note>, when there is a "loss of day"—meaning the day is at its shortest—at that very same time, there is an "increase of day" in the **Region of the Demons** <note>the South</note>, meaning the day is at its longest. Conversely, when the day decreases in the Region of the Gods... ॥ 55 ॥

This is the primordial state of **Vishnu** <note>referring to the sun or the cosmic order</note> in the upper portion. At the **beginning of Aries** <term>Mesha; the first sign of the zodiac, marking the vernal equinox</term>, there is a great increase [in day length] for those where the sun is high. At the **beginning of Libra** <term>Tula; the sign marking the autumnal equinox</term>, the opposite increase occurs. Because of the nature of the Gods' division, it is said that the day is measured accordingly... ॥ 58 ॥ 

In the region of the Gods, there is no constant slipping away, nor is the motion always the same. Due to the reversal of the days, it means the day becomes longer. At the **time of sunrise** <note>original: "udayakale"</note>, for those people... it is not more than the circle. Even there, in the case of a longer day, that is the name...

### The Sun's Motion in the Polar Regions

->[Verse] 48. In that very part of the terrestrial world, among the **Gods** <note>the inhabitants of the North Pole</note> and the **Asuras** <note>the inhabitants of the South Pole</note>, [the Sun] is seen above [the horizon]. Moving northward during its own course... 48.<-

In the **Region of the Gods** <note>original: "Deva-bhaga"</note> and the **Region of the Asuras** <note>original: "Asura-bhaga"</note>, the Sun is seen above the **Earth's circle** <term>Bhumandala; the plane of the horizon or the terrestrial sphere</term>. When the Sun is situated in **Aries** <note>original: "Me[sha]"</note> and subsequent signs, it gradually moves and revolves above the orb of that region. 

Specifically, in the **Region of the Gods**, this occurs during the **Northern Progress** <term>Uttarayana; the half of the year when the Sun moves north from the celestial equator</term>. Conversely, in the **Region of the Asuras**, the Sun is seen revolving above the orb during the **Southern Progress** <term>Dakshinayana; the half of the year when the Sun moves south</term>. 48.

### The Behavior of Shadows

He now describes the behavior of the **shadow** <note>original: "Chhaya"</note>.

->[Verse] 49. The shadow of these two [regions] goes south and north, yet it also moves facing **Meru** <note>the sacred mountain at the North Pole, representing the Earth's axis</note> in their respective parts... 49.<-

In the aforementioned regions of the **Gods** and **Asuras**, which are separated by their respective locations, the shadow appears to the south and north. In these two places, whether the tip of the shadow moves toward the north or the south is determined by the Sun's position relative to the center. 

In the regions of the **Gods** and **Asuras**, the shadow is said to be "facing **Meru**" <note>original: "Meror-abhimukha"</note>. Because the **Asura region** <note>original: "Daitya-bhaga"</note> is located in the southern part, the tip of the shadow there moves specifically toward the south, directed toward the center of their respective location. 49.

### Now, the cause of the planets' rotation is stated.

The **Provector Wind** <term>Pravaha-anila; in ancient Indian astronomy, this is an invisible, powerful wind that constantly drives the entire celestial shell from east to west</term> causes the **Wheel of Stars** <term>Bhachakra; the zodiac or the fixed firmament</term> to revolve. The planetary orbits are held within it in their respective order. 72.

The meaning is as follows: The sphere of the wheel of stars is impelled and thrown from all sides by the **Provector Winds**. Driven by that driving wind, it revolves incessantly and constantly in the sky with a **westward motion** <note>original: "pashchima-gatya"</note>. The wise understand that the orbits of the planets are tied to this celestial sphere. Here, the planetary orbits move in sequence, one below the other, at a rapid pace. Because the planetary orbits are attached to the celestial sphere, they move by the very rotation of that sphere. This is the intended meaning. 73.

For a planet situated in a **great orbit** <note>original: "mahatya kakshaya"; likely referring to the corrected OCR "kattaya"</note>, the divisions of that large circle are themselves large. For a planet situated in a **small orbit**, the divisions are small. 25.

Now, what is to be said next? To this, he provides the answer:

"Multiplied by the minutes of arc, divided by the **circumference of the Earth** <term>mahī-maṇḍala</term>, and adjusted by the hypotenuse... the planet is moved." 84.

When this is applied, the minutes of the planets are divided by the **hypotenuse** <term>karṇa; in Indian astronomy, this refers to the variable distance from the Earth to the planet</term>. Multiplied by the Earth's yojanas, this results in the **diameter** <term>vyāsa</term> of that planet's hypotenuse. From this, the **planetary disk** <term>graha-bimba; the visible circular face of a celestial body</term> is calculated, which is seen at the end of the line of sight—meaning the interval between the observer on Earth and the planet's position in the sky. 84.

First, he describes the **fast-motion epicycle of Mercury** <term>Budha-śīghra-cakra; the mathematical circle used to account for the planet's faster orbital components</term>:

"The light is established by victory... for Mercury and Venus..." 85.

The value for the **fast-motion cycle** <term>vedarūpa-kattā</term> is 32,400.
Then, half of that for the fast-motion cycle of Mercury is 15,320. 85.

...therefore, because of the smallness of a small orbit <note>original: "svalpa-kakṣā"</note>, the swift motion of **Saturn** <note>original: "śani"</note> is known as its revolution <note>original: "bhagaṇa"</note>. If a planet completes its journey in a short time, it is said to experience its "enjoyment" or path <note>original: "bhoga"</note> quickly. 

This is the meaning: therefore, because it is situated the highest among all the planets and moves with the least speed, it is called **Saturn** <note>original: "śanaiścara," literally "the slow-mover"</note>. This is the traditional explanation. Therefore, if its motion is restricted or minimal, its speed is considered non-existent or negligible. In the order of the half-orbits, the planetary motion is established as such. 77.

Now he demonstrates the method for determining the lords of the days, months, and years:

"Descending in order from the highest, the lords of every fourth day are found; similarly, the Moon <note>original: "śaśin"</note> is declared, and the third in the same manner."

In ascending order from Saturn, the lords of the months are remembered. In descending order from the Sun <note>original: "sūrya"</note>, they are established accordingly. 75. <note>The text outlines the 'Hora' system where planetary hours determine the ruler of the day by skipping three planets to reach the fourth.</note>

Below Saturn, in the order of the orbits, the lords of the fourth day occur. The meaning is this: first is **Saturn** <note>original: "śani"</note> itself; then from Saturn, the fourth orbit belongs to the **Moon** <note>original: "candra"</note>. Thus, in this specific order, the lords of the days are **Saturn** (Saturday), the **Sun** (Sunday), the **Moon** (Monday), **Mars** <note>original: "bhauma"</note> (Tuesday), **Mercury** <note>original: "budha"</note> (Wednesday), **Jupiter** <note>original: "guru"</note> (Thursday), and **Venus** <note>original: "śukra"</note> (Friday). 

According to the previously mentioned method of determining the days, by taking every third orbit, the lords are: **Mars**, **Venus**, **Moon**, **Jupiter**, **Sun**, and **Mercury**. Thus, in the order of the half-orbits, the lords of the months are the **Moon**, the **Sun**, **Venus**, and **Mercury**. 79.

Now, he describes the method for bringing forth the motion <note>original: "gati"</note> in the form of leagues:

"The Orbit of the Sky, divided by the revolutions of a specific planet in a Kalpa, and then divided by the number of **Earth-days** <term>Kuvāsara<gloss>a civil day measured from sunrise to sunrise</gloss></term>, is remembered as the universal daily motion for all planets." 82.

This means the Sky-orbit, divided by the planet's own revolutions in a Kalpa, becomes that planet's specific orbit in this context. That same orbit, divided by the number of Earth-days, becomes the motion in leagues traveled daily by all the planets. Through this calculation of motion, the planets are seen to be equal in their respective directions. 82.

### On the Secret Mechanism

Now, he describes another method: ॥ One should prepare the **Celestial Sphere** <term>Gola-yantra<gloss>a mechanical model of the heavenly bodies</gloss></term> by incorporating the **Fierce Seed** <term>Ugra-vija<gloss>a technical code name for mercury (quicksilver), used here as a motive fluid</gloss></term>. For that reason, the one who has attained the feet of the teacher and is skilled in the knowledge of the sphere, constructs a beautiful globe using those instructions not explicitly written. This indeed is the method for the **Self-Moving Construction** <note>original: "svayam-sadhanam," suggesting a form of automated or perpetual motion</note> of the sphere. ॥ 

In age after age, this entire knowledge was lost; now it is revealed. He in whom the grace of the Guru resides will understand it through the effort of those instructions, and not through any other means. This is the meaning. 18 ॥

### The Calculation of Shadows

The self-study of the **Secret Doctrine of Astrology** <term>Jyotishastra-Upanishad</term>, which acts as a light for the deep explanation of the examples of darkness, is now completed. 

### Now, the Chapter on Measurement is explained through questions and answers regarding the sun's measure. ॥ 3 ॥

The nine systems of measurement are:
1. **Brahma** <term>Brahma-mana</term> <note>time as measured by the creator god, Brahma</note>
2. **Divine** <term>Divya-mana</term> <note>time as measured by the gods</note>
3. **Ancestral** <term>Pitrya-mana</term> <note>time as measured by the spirits of the ancestors</note>
4. **Prajapatya** <term>Prajapatya-mana</term> <note>time associated with the lords of creatures</note>
5. **Jupiter’s** <term>Guru-mana</term> <note>time based on the orbit of the planet Jupiter</note>
6. **Solar** <term>Saura-mana</term> <note>time based on the sun's movement through the zodiac</note>
7. **Terrestrial** <term>Savana-mana</term> <note>the daily time from sunrise to sunrise</note>
8. **Lunar** <term>Chandra-mana</term> <note>time based on the phases of the moon</note>
9. **Sidereal** <term>Nakshatra-mana</term> <note>time based on the stars</note> 
These are indeed the nine measurements. 1 ॥

The **Brahma** measurement was mentioned previously in the discussion of the **Kalpa** <note>a vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> and the "Day of Brahma." The **Divine** measurement is second; it is described here as the measurement of the gods. The **Ancestral** measurement is the third, where one lunar month constitutes a single day and night for the ancestors. The fourth is **Prajapatya**, which relates to human-scaled cosmic time. The fifth is the measurement of **Jupiter** <term>Brihaspati</term>, which is defined by the planet's average movement through one zodiac sign. The sixth is the **Solar** measurement, which is defined by the sun's transit. The seventh is the **Terrestrial** <term>Savana</term> measurement, created by the rising of the sun. The eighth is the **Lunar** measurement, defined by the lunar month. The ninth measurement is the **Sidereal**, which is determined by the observation of the **Lunar Mansions** <term>Nakshatra</term>. These are the nine measurements. 2 ॥

Regarding this, some explain the answer to the second question for the sake of daily transactions <term>vyavahara</term> <note>practical or legal usage</note>, applying it to the appropriate times:

> In this world, the four measurements used for practical affairs are the **Solar**, **Lunar**, **Sidereal**, and **Terrestrial**. The sixty-year cycle, however, is always determined by the movement of **Jupiter**. 3 ॥

In the world of humans, transactions are conducted using these four measurements: Solar, Lunar, Sidereal, and Terrestrial. These are the standards for the gods and others as well. 

One might ask: "Are there not five measurements used, starting with the Terrestrial?" Here, the Solar and Lunar are grouped with the Prajapatya, and are used constantly...

Always by the **Terrestrial** <term>Savana</term> <note>original: "savana"; the measurement of a day from sunrise to sunrise</note> measurement, and never by any other—this is the intended meaning. ॥ 2 ॥

### Now, he demonstrates the Solar measurement for practical application.

By the **Solar** <term>Saura</term> measure, in the measurement of day and night, one determines the **Shadashitimukha** <term>Shadashitimukha</term> <note>literally "Eighty-six-mouthed"; a recurring 86-day period used to time specific offerings</note> periods, the **Solstices** <term>Ayana</term>, the **Equinoxes** <term>Vishuvat</term>, and the **Auspicious Time** <term>Punyakala</term> for the **Sun's Transit** <term>Sankranti</term> <note>the moment the sun moves from one zodiac sign to the next</note>. 3 ॥

The term "day and night" refers to the measurement of the complete daily cycle; likewise, the *Shadashitimukha* periods are determined. Also, the two **Solstices**—the southern and northern paths—and the **Equinoxes** situated within those paths. 
On the days when the Sun enters **Aries** <term>Mesha</term> or **Libra** <term>Tula</term>, as well as the **Auspicious Time of Transit**, the meaning is that these events are calculated through the **Solar** measurement starting from that day. 3 ॥

### Now he describes the *Shadashitimukha*.

Starting from **Libra** <term>Tula</term> and proceeding through six signs in sequence, the *Shadashitimukha* occurs; and this takes place specifically within the **Dual signs** <term>Dvisvabhava</term> <note>the zodiac signs Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces, which are considered to have a fluctuating or "double" nature</note>. 4 ॥

For the purpose of counting eighty-six (86) days beginning from **Libra**, there are twenty-eight (28) days and a half-month <note>The text is calculating how 86-day cycles land within the solar months</note>. 
There, one *Shadashitimukha* occurs. Then, in the counting of another eighty-six (86) days, fourteen (14) degrees of **Virgo** <term>Kanya</term> are reached; there, the fourth *Shadashitimukha* takes place. 4 ॥

And this is exactly how it occurs within the **Dual signs**. 5 ॥

### Now he explains this very clearly:

The 26th part <note>degree</note> of **Sagittarius** <term>Dhanu</term>, the 22nd part of **Gemini** <term>Mithuna</term>, and the 14th degree in **Virgo** <term>Kanya</term>. 5 ॥
Having reached these specific points, the calculation is clear. 5 ॥

Now, the *Shadashitimukha* periods have been described. Following that, the days during which the Sun travels through the ten named signs are auspicious for performing ritual bathing and charitable giving <term>snana-dana</term>. Thus, he provides the example of the sign of **Virgo**. ॥ ॥
